items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Honourable members, I have much pleasure in informing the House
that a parliamentary delegation from the Na tional Assembly of Viet Nam, led by Mr
Nguyen Van Hien, Chairman of the Committee on Judiciary, is present in the gallery. I
am sure members would wish that the delegation be welcomed.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: When the House resumes on
Tuesday, 24 July the Government will comp lete the Dairy Industry Restructuring
Amendment Bill and a number of first readings on the Order Paper, including the
Families Commission Amendment Bill and the Companies and Limited Partnerships
Amendment Bill. Wednesday is a members’ day. The Business Committee has also
determined that the House will take extended hours on Wednesday, 25 July, effective
from 9 a.m. on Thursday, 26 July, for the third readings of the Maraeroa A and B
Blocks Claims Settlement Bill and the Maraeroa A and B Blocks Incorporation Bill, the
Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill, the Ng āti Mākino Claims Settlement Bill, and
the Rongowhataata Claims Settlement Bill.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Can I ask the Leader of the

items.speaker: House two questions
items.text: first of a ll, to confirm that those third readings will run into the
afternoon of Thursday next week, as well as the extended Wednesday; and, also, to give
an assurance, as far as the following week is concerned, that if we do go on to the liquor
legislation, there will be plenty of notice because of the conscience vote nature of it?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Two things. I thank the
shadow Leader of the House for those questi ons. It is a good opportun ity to clarify that
under the Standing Orders the Government, by agreement with the Business Committee,
in this case will call for extended hours on Wednesday, 25 July, because what we are
doing is extending the Wednesday into the Thur sday. In effect, we will deal with those
bills on Thursday morning, running through into the afternoon. Ther e will still be a
question time. I will shortly seek leave for the House to sit beyond the 6 o’clock mark,
should we require it, to complete those third readings.
On the issue of the alcohol bill, there are a number of points in the bill that will be of
interest to members across the House. I thin k it is desirable that we have a broad
discussion at the Business Committee. My proposal  is that we will have that discussion
next Tuesday—and I will try to get some information to members of the committee
prior to that time—when we might get some agreement on how we could satisfy
everybody’s requirements around that debate.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: So that we get everything
done in sequence, I will now seek leave th at should the debate on the bills that the
Business Committee has agreed will be dea lt with under extended hours next week
progress beyond 6 o’clock on the Thursday, th e House will continue beyond 6 o’clock
for the conclusion of the third readings.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I think we also indicated that we might deal with some flexibility around the 1
o’clock time, if we were coming to the end of the debate on one of those bills.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: That is true. We essentially
are splitting the debate on these five bill s into morning and afternoon sessions. I think
the leave should be that if either of those sessions requires the House to sit for a short
time beyond the normal rising time, we should do so until the conclusion of the debate
on the bill in progress.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Water Rights—Prime Minister’s Statements
1. GRANT ROBERTSON (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Prime Minister :
Does he stand by all his statements regarding water ownership, rights and interests?
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister)  on behalf of the Prime Minister:
Yes.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Can he confirm the joint announcem ent he made last night with
the M āori Party leadership that no matter what the outcome of the tribunal and
subsequent court action, he will not legislate, even if that outcome was that M āori had a
proprietary-type right over water?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Prime Minister stands by the statements made in the
statement that was released.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Can he confirm that his agreem ent to not legislate against M āori
rights and interests in water has, in fact , already been broken by the Mixed Ownership
Model Bill, which has passed through Parliame nt and allows for th e partial sale of
entities like Mighty River Power th at have rights and interests in water that affect all
New Zealanders, including Māori?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, the Mixed Ownership Model Bill does not do that. In
fact, it includes the preservation of section 9 of the State-Owned Enterprises Act and its
references to the Treaty of Waitangi. What th e Prime Minister is doing is quite different
from what the previous Labour Government di d, and that is we are building confidence
around discussion with Māori about their rights and interests, rather than overreacting—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That was beyond the question asked.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Can he confirm that it is hi s Government’s intention that no
matter what the outcome of the Waitangi  Tribunal and subsequent court action—
whatever rights it may decide M āori have in terms of water—his Government will not
legislate in that regard?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Prime Minister stands by the statement in the statement
that was released last night. It is the Gove rnment’s expectation that—well, put it this
way: the member is probably not correctly  connecting any outcome from the Waitangi
Tribunal with any outcome from the court action, because the court action is much more
likely to be focused on preventing the sale of assets going ahead, rather than any
particular aspect of Māori rights and interests.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does he agree with Tariana Turia that it was a misconception that
this claim is about the owne rship of water; if so, why did he continue to make
statements about his opposition to the ownershi p of water, if not to  just raise tension
around the issue?
19 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 3747

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The issue of ownership was actually raised by the claimants.
In fact, we have seen claimants, I thi nk, discussing it publicly  recently. The Prime
Minister stands by his restatement of the longstanding view of New Zealand’s
Governments and jurisprudence that no one owns the water.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: In light of the indemnity granted for Treaty matters to private
shareholders of the to-be-privatised State-owned enterprises under the mixed ownership
model legislation passed recently, does that mean that all risk from court action now lies
with the Crown; if so, why did his Minister of Finance not record that unspecified fiscal
risk as part of the Budget documentation currently being considered by the House?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It has always been the case that the risks or costs associated
with Treaty settlements are matters between the Crown and iwi. But,  again, I think this
member, like the other, is getting ahead of himself over whether or not the courts are
likely to be settling the issue of M āori rights and interests. There is a prospect of court
action. That court action is much more likely to be related to injuncting the sale process.
It is unlikely that the courts them selves would set out to determine M āori rights and
interests. If they did, that could take quite a long time.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is it correct that the reasons he raised the spectre of ownership of
water by M āori were to divert pub lic attention from his hugely unpopular asset sales
programme and to inflame divisions about Treaty issues, and when will he apologise for
this divisive behaviour?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think the member is overstating his case there. The fact is
claimants have gone to the tribunal, they ha ve made a range of claims, and some of
them have expressed those claims as owners hip of the water. The Prime Minister just
clearly restated, in the light of that action in the tribunal, what the longstanding position
of New Zealand Governments has been, and it will remain so. Obviously, there is pretty
broad public interest in whether the Waitangi Tribunal is or is not going to be contesting
the ownership of water.
State-owned Energy Companies and Air New Zealand, Sales—Cost as at July 2012
2. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green) to the Minister of Finance: What
has been the total cost to date of exte nding and implementing the Government’s asset
sales programme, which it calls the Mixed Ownership Model?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As I said in answer to a similar
question last month, the total amounts of th e contracts are commercially sensitive
because the Government intends to renegotia te those contracts fo r each partial share
offer. I can confirm that about $1.1 million has been paid out so far, pursuant to
communication, marketing, market research, an d advertising servic es. But I would say
to the member that the Government has been  quite open about the potential costs of the
programme. These are expected to be about 2 percent of the tota l programme proceeds,
which by any market standard is quite low.  Other share floats generally have costs
somewhere between 3 to 7 percent of the total proceeds.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does the figure of $1.1 million so far include all the costs of the
asset sales policy, including contracting fo r advertising and communications, banks and
sharebrokers, legal advisers, independent advisers, policy work conducted by the Public
Service, and activities not covered by the appr opriations within Vote Finance, such as
pre-sale preparation by the energy co mpanies, work conducted by Government
departments other than Treasury, and the Waitangi Tribunal hearing costs?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, it does not. It refers to the amount that has been paid out
under the kinds of contracts th at the member has referred to  in the past. I must say,
though, that a good deal of the Public Service activity has been very useful because it
has shown up aspects of the operations of th e companies that can be improved. In the
3748 Questions for Oral Answer 19 Jul 2012
case of Māori rights and interests, it has flushe d out a number of issues, some of which
should have been resolved some time ago, and have not been, and others of which have
been publicly discussed. So that expenditure I would regard as pretty useful, even if
there was no sale.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The primary question that
was put down was general. It asked what has b een the total cost to date. It did not refer
just to the contracting costs around advertisi ng and communications. It  also referred to
all costs, including the Public Service wor k. The Minister has just confirmed in his
answer there that his answer to the primary question did no t include those other costs,
yet this was a question set down on notice. It did not sp ecify just advertising and
communication. It was very broad.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I listened to the Minister’s  answer very carefully. What he
said was that some of the costs relating to certain contracts were considered
commercially sensitive, and he did not believe it was in the public interest to identify all
of those. In respect of the departmental co sts, it is possible the Minister interpreted
those the way many would—that the departmental officials have to be paid anyhow and
there is no particular additional cost, depe nding on what work they are doing. It is not
often in costing projects like this that the departmental costs are included. If the member
had wanted that to be incl uded in such a figure, maybe he should have been more
specific in the question.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Can the Minister of Finance, then, provide us with the true cost,
including departmental costs, of preparing the asset sales programme and implementing
this policy agenda from the Government?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Depending on what the member means by “the true cost”.
We can certainly provide over time the direct costs of the share float. I suppose if we
were going to take a broader vi ew of what the costs are, th en we would need to also
weigh that up against the be nefits of improving the opera tion of the companies and
getting on and resolving outstanding M āori claims that have been brought to the fore by
this process, because those are, clearly, benefits to the Government and to the country.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Given that the Prime Minister has conceded that there
could be a delay in the float of Mighty Rive r Power, does he think that it is wise to
continue spending hundreds of thousands of taxpayers’ dollars, and potentially millions,
on the asset sales process when a change in circumstances, such as a legal challenge,
could mean that much of the work would ha ve to be repeated and/or amended, costing
the taxpayer further hundreds of thousands of dollars or, potentially, millions of dollars?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As the member will know, the statements made by the Prime
Minister indicate that it is pos sible that the share sales coul d be delayed. Th at is yet to
be proven. We have not had the conclusions of the Waitangi Tribunal. We have not had
anyone rebut the Government’s proposition that the sale of shares does not compromise
its ability to deal with iwi claims. So we ha ve yet to see whether there can be successful
claims in the tribunal, and, then, yet to see whether ther e can be a successful court
action. The likelihood of that is there. It is probably low.  We are proceeding with the
pre-sale process.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Has the Minister sought any official advice on the impact on the
asset sales revenue of the uncertainty created by potential court action over water rights;
if so, what advice has he received?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I do not think we have asked specifically for that advice.
There has been some discussion about it. On e indication of the potential impact on
value, I am advised, is that there has been no change in the share price of TrustPower or
Contact Energy, both of which are operating in  the same markets as the State-owned
enterprises and are potentiall y interested in the same kinds of claims. We have
19 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 3749
confidence that the process we have been involved in for the last 2 or 3 years of
discussing these matters with M āori is a process that can l ead to a solution, and that
tribunal claims and court actions are unlikely to make solutions more achievable.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does the Minister concede that there could be a cost on energy
companies as a result of the recognition of iwi rights to water—that  there would be an
impact on the profitability of those companies were such recognition to be followed
through in the courts or through an agreem ent between Crown and iwi—and that that
should be factored into how much he thinks he is going  to raise by selling the
companies?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I do not concede that. The member is asking these
questions as if these issues are all new. In fact, they are not. One of  the first actions of
this Government was to renegotiate the Waikato River settlement, which was a
settlement of freshwater claims related to the river, which has more dams on it than any
other river in New Zealand. That settlement di d deal with Tainui’s rights and interests
and had no impact on the operation of the electricity companie s that have dams on that
river.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he agree with the Prime Minister that as many as three
asset sales could occur in th e coming year or two, in light  of Forsyth Barr research
showing that the asset sales would need to be  spread out over 5 years to let the capital
markets absorb them and to maximise the revenue to the Crown?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: People will have their own view s about it. It is our view, in
the light of the fact New Zealanders are saving more than they have in the last 20 or 30
years, and are paying down debt because of record low interest rates, that there will be a
large pool of cash and demand for these floats. The Government as it goes will make
decisions about the timing of them, but we are a bit more optimistic than Forsyth Barr.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given that the Government has stated that sales would not go
ahead if market conditions were unfavourab le, has the Government determined what
conditions would be unfavourable; if so, what are they?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, we have not determined what conditions would be
unfavourable. You can imagine various scenarios—some positive, some negative. The
fact that interest rates are the lowest they ha ve ever been is probably tending to increase
the value of utility compan ies on the one hand; on the ot her hand, if there was some
serious meltdown in Europe and financial markets shut down, then clearly that would be
negative. But those are judgments we would make closer to the time.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given the risk created by uncertainty over water rights, the cost
of an accelerated sales programme, and the c ontinuing volatility in sharemarkets, is not
the fiscally responsible course of action fo r the Government to suspend asset sales at
this time?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Not for those reasons on their ow n. The fact is that all of
those conditions apply regardless of the sale. M āori are asserting right s and interests in
water. Whoever owns those companies, thos e rights and interests would need to be
resolved. If there is uncertainty generate d by those claims, then there would be
uncertainty for State-owned enterprises, or for 51 percent Government-owned State-
owned enterprises. So the fact that M āori have made claims make s, in that sense, no
difference to who owns them. If there is uncertainty there for the private investors, there
is uncertainty there for the Government. Thos e claims are ones that we are focused on
resolving, as we have resolved a number of th em in the last couple of years, and we are
continuing to discuss the outstanding claims.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If he is so confident of New Zealand mums and dads
having sufficient savings to take up the shar e offer, why on earth is he floating these
shares on the Australian market?
3750 Questions for Oral Answer 19 Jul 2012

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, we are not.
Government Financial Position—Financial Statements for 11 Months Ended 31
May 2012
3. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Minister of Finance :
What reports has he received on the Government’s financial position?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Earlier this month Treasury
published the Government’s Financial Stat ements for the 11 months ending 31 May.
The Government’s operating balance was about $1.1 billion better than forecast at
minus $5.9 billion. This is slightly encour aging, but the global environment remains
uncertain and there will continue to be fluctuations in the tax take from month to month.
The world situation, though, rein forces the need for the G overnment to keep a firm
control on its costs.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: How does balancing the Government’s books help the economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I know that it is broadly accepted in the National Party that it
is good for the economy, but I would like to e xplain the reasons why to Opposition
members, because they remain unconvinced. Balancing the books is one of the most
important things a Government can do to  build the resilience of our economy and
reduce its vulnerability to growing overseas indebtedness, and take the pressure off
interest rates and the exchange rate. For in stance, the average business lending rate has
now fallen to 6.04 percent at May 2012, compar ed with 9.4 percent in late 2008. In so
far as the Government is on track to surp lus, this helps make our businesses more
competitive.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: How is the Government’s responsible management of its finances—
[Interruption]—helping New Zealand’s households?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Did the Minister hear the question?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, I did.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Because the Speaker did not.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Again, for the benefit of those who want to borrow more and
spend more, balancing the books helps take pr essure off mortgage interest rates. The
average residential floating rate is currently 5.9 percent, compared with a floating rate
of almost 11 percent in late 2008. For a family with a $200,000 mortgage, that is a
saving of around $200 per week, or more than $10,000 per year, since they elected a
National Government.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does today’s report from Statis tics New Zealand show that the
Government’s finances need to provide fo r more than 1 million people over 65 years of
age by the end of the 2020s, and what change s to superannuation is he intending to
make to ensure that New Zealanders have fair and sustainable superannuation?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think the member probably put it correctly when he said
the economy needs to be able to support a growing number of older people. We are
focusing very strongly on reinforcing the competitiveness and productivity of this
economy so that it can support an olde r population. As the member knows, the
Government’s position on national superannuation is quite clear.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What other approaches to managing the Government’s finances is he
aware of?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I have heard a number of reports of propositions that would
require a considerable amount of extra debt  and unsustainable spending: for instance,
borrowing to pay for reducing the retirement age to 60 for some workers, borrowing to
pay for the Auckland rail loop, borrowing to pa y for doubling paid parental leave, and,
of course, borrowing $5 billion to $7 billion on global financial markets to buy back the
four State-owned enterprises that the Government plans to partially sell.
19 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 3751

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does his Budget project that by the end of the 2016 year his
Government, if still in office, would be sp ending more on superannuation than on all of
education—that is, more th an on preschool, primary, in termediate, secondary, and
tertiary education combined—if so, how can  he deny that changes are necessary and
should be signalled now, rather than sprung on people later?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That may be the case with th e Budget projections; I would
need to check it. As far as I know, no one  is proposing—or maybe they are proposing
that. Maybe the Opposition is proposing to somehow reduce national superannuation, so
that by 2016 we are spending less  on it than on educa tion. If so, people need to be told
about that, so that it is not sprung on them as a surprise.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Why is the Minister braggi ng about a floating rate of 5
percent when that equivalent rate in the EU, the UK, and Japan is four times less than
that?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government is not bragging about anything. It is simply
pointing out that the floating rate of intere st is around about half what it was in 2008,
which is giving New Zealanders the opportunity  to pay off debt an d save more money,
and those are good things for the economy.
Welfare Reforms—Transition Process for Initiatives Targeting Young People
4. JACINDA ARDERN (Labour)  to the Minister for Social Development : Does
she stand by her statement that  “you need to look at the 16 and 17-year-olds and for the
very first time our focus is keenly going on them”?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Yes, and that is why
we are making significant changes to ensure that we are focused on getting more 16 and
17-year-olds into education, training, or work-based learning, and not going on to a
benefit.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Can she genuinely maintain she has a keen focus on young people,
when school-leavers with no plans have steppe d into a black hole, given that she has
shut down Youth Transition Services, and the replacement services have had their start
date changed by her yet again and will not be opening their doors until at least the end
of August?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I believe that those services  are continuing to work with
those young people, so they ar e getting those services. Bu t on 20 August that will be
changing.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Is it acceptable for her to tell Youth Transition Services to continue
operating when they have not got a contract with the Ministry of Social Development,
when many schools still do not know the inform ation they are meant to be providing to
them, and when the legislation underpinning the whole thing, including privacy issues,
still has not been passed?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I have a number of bits of good news for the member.
The legislation will be passed this afternoon, so that is going well and is all on track.
Then we have a notice period where we are going to those young people and making
sure they know what is happening. The ot her part of it is th at the schools are not
actually providing that information directly; it is coming from the national office with
ENROL. So it is quite straightforward for us to be extracting the information we need
and to be using it accordingly.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Is she asking Youth Transition Services to operate without a
contract and without a mandate?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: It is quite common for contracts to roll over and continue
on. That is what happens quite often. There is often a gap between what was going to be
an end date and then a new date. It happened under Labour. It is happening under
3752 Questions for Oral Answer 19 Jul 2012
National. It is quite normal for it to happen, and that is what is happening in this
instance.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Does her keen focus include her staff instructing Youth Transition
Services that, no matter what, it cannot refe r young people to Work and Income, even
when some youth services bran ches are meant to now servic e these needs with just one
office and few experienced staff, and are covering geographic areas equivalent to half
the South Island?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: As we go through the transi tion we are going to have
Work and Income staff actually in those offi ces. So they will not have to refer them
there; they will have a staff member on site who will be able to work with them. So we
are, obviously, conscious of what the changes are that are coming up and what needs to
be done. We are working closely with them. The feedback I am getting is how positive
it is and how much they are looking forward to the work that is going on.
Welfare Reforms—Reducing Long-term Welfare Dependence
5. MIKE SABIN (National—Northland) to the Minister for Social Development:
How will the Government’s welfare reforms support people off welfare and into work?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I am absolutely
thrilled that our reforms are going to fundamentally change  the way that welfare is
delivered. The Social Security (Youth Support and Work Focus) Amendment Bill,
which is set to have its third reading just this afternoon, means that we will be working
with youth, but also with, predominantl y, women on welfare, far better than we
currently do. These changes will introduce gr eater work expectations and preparation,
as well as a real wraparound service for those young people who so desperately need it
and in the past have not been receiving it.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: What are the aims of these welfare reforms?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The statistics have been tel ling us for years that welfare
dependence is intergenerational. One hundr ed and seventy thous and New Zealanders
have spent most of the last decade on welfare. We simply cannot continue to spend $8
billion a year to support 12 percent of the working-age population. These reforms are
aimed at addressing the causes of dependen ce, and at having people work-ready, with
greater support for young people, some sole parents, widows, and women alone.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: What other work has been done to date on welfare reform?

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Heaps.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Heaps, as my colleague says behind me. It started with
Future Focus in 2010, which we have seen a huge success with. We are now following
up with this bill, which, as I say, has its focus predominantly on youth but also on some
of those on the DPB. The third bill is yet to go through this year but is well on its way, I
am pleased to advise the House. That bill will include significant changes that will
completely reform the way that welfare is delivered.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Can she confirm, based on her own department’s projections in the
Budget, that even after the implementati on of her $287 million reforms the number of

items.text: Good news. The
Government is funding a postg raduate intern programme fo r 70 students in areas such
as engineering, design, and information a nd communications tec hnology to work in
some of New Zealand’s most innovative busine sses. This opportunity provides valuable
work experience in a commercial environm ent and demonstrates  potential industry-

items.text: A number of provisions from
Fresh Start, which was introduced 2 years a go, have allowed the Youth Court to give
more flexible and more effective resolutions  and orders. This has resulted in far less
churn of young people going through youth jus tice residences, and 50 percent fewer
young people going from the Youth Court into the District Court for sentencing.

items.speaker: Dr Jackie Blue
items.text: What other positive youth justice trends is he aware of?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: I am aware of statistics released by the Ministry of

22 percent, and court appearances are down 19 percent—this is the group of highest-end

SOCIAL SECURITY (YOUTH SUPPORT AND WORK FOCUS) AMENDMENT
BILL
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I move, That the
Social Security (Youth Support and Work Focus) Amendmen t Bill be now read a third
time. Doing nothing about benefit dependency is no longer an option. For too long the
system has let thousands of New Zealande rs languish on benefits, with no hope, no
support, and no encouragement to live and lead a better life. In fact , the welfare system
itself has failed too many New Zealanders. This Government will not stand by and let
that continue. The bill be fore the House today con tinues the significant and
comprehensive reforms this Government has introduced to modernise the welfare
system. It started with Future Focus in 2010 an d we are following it up with this bill,
before introducing a third tranche of welfare reform later this year that will contain the
most significant changes.
The changes we are making will reset ob ligations and expect ations, introducing a
level of fairness that is long overdue. The statistics have been  telling us for years that
welfare dependence is intergenerational. This causes a loss of hope and a lack of
ambition for adults and for their children  in so many ways. One hundred and seventy
thousand New Zealanders have spent most of  the last decade on welfare. You cannot
tell me that that is good for them as i ndividuals, good for their families, or, certainly,
any good for their children. We simply cannot continue to spend up to $8 billion a year
to support 12 percent of the working-age population. I cannot ask taxpayers to support a
system that continually grows, but does not address the causes of dependence, at the
expense of health, education, and other priorities that taxpayers might like us to make.
I am not convinced that the left sees a pr oblem with this level of dependence, but I
am convinced there is a difference in philo sophy when it comes to welfare. The left
creates dependence; the right creates indepe ndence. We would rather give them the
tools and the support to be independent. The right will incentivise, while the left are
busy with sympathising. This is not about a lack of compassion. I have a huge amount
of respect for people who are raising their families with little money. I just want them to
have more. We could do nothi ng, as the left would prefer , and that means leaving the
19 Jul 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 3761
320,000 New Zealanders on welfare, with no hope  of a better life. I simply refuse to do
that.
When listening to the debate on these reforms it is clear that some have no faith
whatsoever in the ability of New Zealanders to get off welfare and provide for
themselves. On this side of the House, qui te frankly, we see that as demeaning. We
believe in people and their ability to succeed and better their situation, and we believe in
providing them with the support so that they  can do so. We do not believe in leaving
people on the scrap heap. To continue simp ly paying a 17-year-old sole mother a
weekly sum of money and give her no other support would quite frankly, in my view,
be irresponsible. We will not do that. To wr ite off single women as unable to support
themselves financially, simply because they are women, would be ignorant. We will not
do that. To allow people to just give up and opt out of work would be a failure of any
Government, and we will not do that. National will modernise the welfare system with a
clear work focus that applies to a far greater number of people.
We will take a completely new approach with young people. They will be required to
be in education or training to get a benefit. Their bills will be paid directly. Money for
food will be loaded on to payment cards, inst ead of giving them cash. They will have to
complete budgeting and/or parenting program mes, if appropriate . They will receive
small cash incentives for meeting these milestones. Instead of having a solely financial
relationship with Work and Income, teen pa rents, along with other young people, will
have a youth service provider or private work er working alongside them. That provider
will help them navigate issues like accommodation, bills, getting access to education or
training, and upskilling. Teen parents will ge t vital childcare. We are putting aside $80
million for this, so there is no barrier to th em getting the education or training they
need.
This bill will require sole parents with  children over 14 to look for full-time work,
and will require sole parents with children over 5 to look for part-time work. This bill
will require those parents to start preparing themselves, in advance, for this change.
This bill removes the sexist  and discriminatory policy th at has seen the women alone
and widows benefits existing well beyond a time when they were necessary. These
benefits effectively said that a woman c ould not fend for herself without a man, and I
think that is just archaic. We are modernising welfare. We  are providing more support,
and we will be expecting something back. We have changed the commencement date of
30 July 2012 for the youth package changes to 20 August 2012. Changes to the widows
benefit, women alone benefit, and DPB come into effect in October of this year.
As I have mentioned, the bill introduces a new system of support, obligations, and
financial assistance for young peopl e and teen parents. The aim of this is to balance
support and obligations in a way that will improve social  outcomes for young people.
This is new; it is a different approach to a longstanding problem. Never before has
anyone looked at the benefit pipeline and put such a huge i nvestment into those very
young people who are likely to go on to benefit. Currently, there are around 3,000 16
and 17-year-olds and 16 to 18-year-old  parents on a benefit, and around 14,000 young
people aged 16 to 17 years wh o are considered to be “neets”—not in education,
employment, or training. We are determined to stop the track on to benefit. The changes
in this bill will reduce the risk of long-te rm benefit dependency for teenagers, and
ensure they have better outcomes and opportuni ties. The best way to do this is through
work and training, and we are investing $148 m illion over 4 years for youth services to
achieve this, including that very necessary wraparound support.
The left has criticised this investment a lot. I stand by it. We are going to have youth-
focused providers who are the experts in working with young people, motivating them,
and helping them to turn th eir lives round. We are being fl exible and innovative in how
3762 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  19 Jul 2012
we do that, but uncompromising in the outcomes that we want. There has been some
speculation on the next welfare reform bill.  I would like to assure the House that
progress is being made. As I previously ha ve indicated, amongst other things we will
change the benefit categories, install the i nvestment approach, and put in a regime of
social obligations and drug testing for some beneficiaries.
But in conclusion on the Social Secu rity (Youth Support and Work Focus)
Amendment Bill, I would like to extend some important thankyous—firstly, to Sam
Lotu-Iiga and to those members of the Social Services Committee from all sides of the
House who have worked on the bill. I want to  recognise your work, for sitting during
adjournments, for the time that you gave to people to make their submissions, and for
the suggestions you made for changes to the bill, some of which we were able to take on
board. I know that through th e select committee process the committee actually found a
couple of things that were slightly ambiguous  and suggested we make changes to those
problems. I think we see a better bill for that  process, so I want to thank those members
of the select committee for the time they spent on the bill.
I particularly would like to thank my hard -working officials. There have been many
officials from many departments, but main ly, obviously, those from the Ministry of
Social Development who work in the policy unit, who hopefully are listening out there.
I just say an absolute heartf elt thank you. They really are the engine behind all of this.
They take those ideas and they turn them in to something real, and I want to say thank
you. Treasury has worked really hard. Desp ite the sometimes fun comments I make,
Treasury has actually just got on alongside of this and has been a real part of that robust
debate that I think leads to  a better piece of work. We have had other ministries—
whether it be the Ministry of Health, the Inland Revenue Department, or the Ministry of
Education, in particular—that have helped us . Their role in this has been absolutely
critical, so I do say a real, genuine thank you.
I also say thank you to Cabine t. I say thank you to Cabine t because it is actually
putting in that huge investment of more th an $148 million. The total costs of this are
$287 million. Cabinet does not do it lightly. I had to go to Cabinet and prove a really
strong case of why this was going to make  a fundamental difference to these young
people—and it does. Change is on the way. I thi nk this is a big part of that brighter
future for New Zealand, and I would like to commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I am pleased to rise on behalf of the Labour Party
and give what I think is a very considered  response from our party to this piece of
legislation, the Social Security (Youth S upport and Work Focus) Amendment Bill, and
to the Government’s welfare reforms generall y. I have said it befo re in this House:
Labour’s approach to reform around welfar e has always been to look through the
perception that is often pe rpetuated by politicians in th is space—dangerously so
sometimes, I would say—and to look to the reality, because we ignore the reality at our
peril. The more that perception is perpetuated, the more we risk our own ability to fulfil
the fundamental principle of doi ng what is right and what wo rks, and that is something
that I will defend staunchly in this area.
If we were to come back to the evidence when it comes to welfare reform, what is
the context in which these reforms are being introduced? Well,  in 2009, when the
Government came in, if you look at the unemployment benefit numbers, we were sitting
at roughly 18,000 people on an unemployment be nefit. We are now looking at almost
50,000 people sitting on an unemployment bene fit. I know that on this matter the

items.speaker: Minister and I will agree
items.text: that has not happened because New Zealanders have had a
sudden change of attitude to work. Ther e has been a change in the economic
environment in New Zealand. Laying aside all of Labour’s views on whether the
Government could and should have done more  on that—laying that aside—there have
19 Jul 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 3763
been economic circumstances that have led to more Kiwis joining the dole queue, and
reluctantly so. I must emphasise that. Unempl oyment is currently at 6.7 percent. We
need only to look in our local areas where a job is advertised and at the enormous
queues that extend outside of, for instance, supermarkets advertising a handful of jobs to
know that Kiwis want to work.
The Minister claims that she believes that , too. Why, then, during this debate, and in
the outside world, have we heard statements like “The dream is over.”, and members in
this House, in this debate, talk about the lifestyle of living on welfare? That kind of
language makes it much more difficult for us to  get to the core of the issue and address
the real barriers that exist for people moving from welfare into work, because there is no
denying that Labour is a believer in work—t he value of work, the dignity that work
provides—and we will do everything we can to assist Kiwis into work.
So what are the barriers to that? Well, at the moment you cannot deny that it is the
availability of work. We have touched on that. But also there was a survey conducted by
the Inland Revenue Department, which we  have referred to consistently, that
demonstrated that the other barriers for people entering into work were the cost of
childcare, and, for 64 percent of people, whether they had the right training and
education to move into the jobs that were  available. So, on those measures, what does
this bill do? On work and on job creation, obvious ly it does very little. It is a social
development bill. But what has the Govern ment done on it? Agai n, it has done very
little. It has not even met its own projecti ons on job creation that were set out by
Treasury. So, on that count, we consider th at the Government ha s not done enough. If
you want to fix welfare, fix the econo my—and on that count we believe the
Government has failed.
The second measure is training and education. If you are under 19 and on a benefit—
if you are a sole parent, for instance—then ther e are some measures in this bill that are
training and education focused, and also if  you are on an independent youth benefit.
But, let us put it into context. That  actually equates to roughly 2,500 to 3,000 young
people on welfare who will be affected by th at. For the vast majority—for instance,
domestic purposes benefit recipients who us ed to be eligible for a training incentive
allowance—that is still gone. All other incentives and support around training and
education do not exist in this bill, so let us be under no illusions there.
On childcare, to an extent the Ministry of  Social Development and the Minister have
acknowledged that this is a barrier, because she has exte nded the childcare subsidy for
1,500 people. The big question we have aske d is, what about the 112,000 who continue
to struggle with that cost? On those measures, this bill will not substantively assist those
who need it the most. So what if you are not 18 or 19? Well, it is very easy, I think, to
be misled by the Minister’s statement. In her last speech alone she said: “the welfare
system itself has failed too many New Zealan ders. The Government will not stand by
and let that continue.”
Show me how you are changing that with this  bill. If you are not 18 or 19 years old
and you are on welfare, all you get from this b ill is more work tes ting. We are asking
what about the rest, Minister? What about the rest? I understand that sh e is targeting 16
and 17-year-olds, but there are hundreds of  thousands on the benefit now, who are not
16 and 17, who need that assistance. She sa ys: “We will not let it continue. We are
modernising the welfare system.” I would like  to see the evidence of that for those who
are on an unemployment benefit, on the DPB, or on the sickness benefit.
If we are looking at those who are on the domestic purposes benefit, for instance, we
have already had a set of reforms brought in by the Minister. We have had Future
Focus, which brought in extra part-time work  testing, and now we have this set of
reforms. But even on the Ministry of Social  Development’s own projections, even after
3764 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  19 Jul 2012
these $287 million reforms are brought in, the number on the domestic purposes benefit
is still projected to be 10,000 higher than when  the Minister started. Surely that raises
some flags over whether or not work testing alone is going to provide what is needed to
make a real difference for those women in particular, because they do represent the
most significant number of people on that form of support.
So we highlight again that if you want to fix welfare, fix the economy but address the
other barriers at the same time. But in the meantime, we do agree to the extent that the
Government is targeting young people. The question becomes how you do it. Again, we
want to come back to th e evidence and the reality on the ground for those who are
already working in the space of Youth Transi tion Services. Now, this bill will assist
14,000 young people. This is what the ministry and the Minister have projected. There
are over 80,000 young people not in employment, education, or training, and they are
not just 16 and 17. We hear d from Youth Transition Se rvices operating on the ground
that 60 percent of the young people they help actually fall off the track after they are 17,
and need some kind of service that is targeted  to their needs and will assist them to get
back into work, training, education, or whatever fits their individual circumstances.
We, instead, have contended that the Gove rnment needed to work with more, not
less, and I will highlight that we are spending more and working with less via this piece
of legislation. We needed to give the exis ting providers who are out there doing a great
job the flexibility th ey needed to take into account the circumstances of the young
person. Some are exiting from school because school was a rough place for them. They
were not on track educationall y. The last thing they want to  do is be shoved back into
school. We have got to try to fit their aspirations with a programme that keeps them on
track. So we wanted to give providers th at flexibility. We did not want to skew
incentives, and we feel that that is what this bill does. Again, always having the best
interests and the sustainability of a young pers on in training in mind, not just short-term
gains, is our approach when it comes to young people.
I want to flag, though, in the concluding remarks of my speech, a fundamental part of
these reforms that has not been canvassed broadly, and that is that this legislation means
that providers in the community—some pr ivate providers—will now be administering
part of the Social Security Act to a degree that we have not seen in New Zealand. If a
young person in need has previously been  dealt with by Work and Income—an
emergency hardship grant or any kind of gran t that Work and Income previously would
have dealt with—that has now been contracted out to th e community. Our concern as
Labour members is what is next. This may be only 2,500 or 3,000 young people, but we
believe that with any partitioning off of the welfare state to community organisations to
a large degree—perhaps the sickness benefit might be next, the invalids benefit—we
have real concerns over that kind of track. I ask the Minister, if that is not part of your
agenda, to stand up and give this House those assurances.
But, in conclusion, I say that Labour is  the party of work. We are the party of
opportunity. We understand the dignity that co mes with work, and that families will
always be better off in work. For us the que stion is how we get there. We do not focus
on rhetoric and perception in this party. We focus on evidence and the reality of what is
happening on the ground, and, in that sense, it is time we went back to true social
security—a dignified system that transitions people into the work they deserve.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: I rise on behalf of the ACT Party to support
the Social Security (Youth Support and Wo rk Focus) Amendment Bill. I start by
congratulating the Minister for Social Develo pment, Paula Bennett, not just on this bill
but on her courage, empathy, and diligence wi th this rather complex portfolio, which
she manages on a day-by-day basis. Her success and her progress is something that
gladdens me. I also give credit to the ch airman of the Social Services Committee and
19 Jul 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 3765
the select committee, but particularly to the leadership of the select committee under the
member Sam Lotu-Iiga—a first-class member  of Parliament doing a great job on that
select committee.
Welfare reform is something that th e ACT Party has long championed. ACT MPs
and supporters have worked hard in the wild erness to bring about welfare reform. This
reform is long overdue. We have made the ca se that our system no longer works, and
that too many New Zealanders are left out of  work, out of hope, and out of dignity by a
system forced upon them. The system can gi ve somebody else’s cold hard cash, but
nothing more, and that is the problem with  socialism: you run out of other people’s
money very quickly.
ACT explained that children and young mothers need love and community—love
and community that a bank transfer at midni ght cannot give. The ACT Party is glad to
see mutual obligation become what everyone in  this House, deep in their soul, knows is
right—mutual obligation. One hopes that one day reforming the Resource Management
Act the Government spending limits become  what everybody knows is right. For now
we are pleased with welfare reform, and welfare reform is  the incremental step to
progress for our country; it is taking people without hope, taking people without a job,
removing the welfare cheque, and giving them  the dignity and oppor tunity to provide
for themselves through work.
Along the way this bill has been champi oned by the ACT Party, supported by the
Welfare Working Group, and I want to tha nk the Welfare Working Group for the hard
work that it has done to contribute to th is. The group found that one in eight working-
age New Zealanders is on some form of  handout, borrowed every week from the
savings of the Swiss, the Germans, and th e Chinese. We cannot continue to borrow on
the backs of our great-grandchildren yet born for a welfare system that fails our youth
today—fails dignity and fails opportunity, fail s hope and fails self-r eliance, fails self-
reliance and fails self-esteem. So in this parliamentary term, welfare reform is supported
not only by ACT but by the recommendations fr om the working group, and is part of
our confidence and supply agreement. This  Minister, this young Minister, who knows
about these matters, these complex matters, has helped it by running it hard.
It is ACT’s vote that makes the reforms possible; it is not the votes of the people
opposite, who will take from the Chinese, th e Swiss, and the Fren ch and spend their
money by borrowing it from them on a welfare system that fails us. It is the ACT’s
confidence and supply agreement that stipulat es the obligations of  parents as per the
Welfare Working Group—the obligations of being a responsible parent. Having
children is a God-given right, but an awesome responsibility, and it needs to be sheeted
home.
ACT’s confidence and supply agreement also  includes initiatives for better support
for at-risk families. It is the at-risk fa milies we need to target through income
management and the contestable provision of social services. The contestable delivery
of social services is critical to the partne rship between the State, which gives the hand
up, and the recipient, who takes the handout. Wh en I was first elected to Parliament 4
decades ago in the electorate of Whangarei, the local police, the local social workers,
and local employers knew everyone in the ci ty. Welfare then could work because in
Whangarei all those years ago we were in it together. Now the State has alienated
people from the social welfare system. So this  bill represents a small step towards that
kind of mutual connectivity and responsibility. The community used to say to people on
welfare: “We will he lp you, but you have a few things to do for yourself.” We do not
hear that any longer. Self-ob ligation brings self-respect, se lf-respect brings self-esteem,
and self-esteem brings dignity. That is what this bill seeks to achieve.
3766 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  19 Jul 2012
The current welfare reforms do not propose a ll stick with no carrot, because you will
not have reform with just stick and no carrot,  but with true mutual obligations. That is
what welfare is about. If we are going to bor row from the savings of others, we have to
have a true mutual obligation that we are going to help ou rselves to help those who are
helping us help ourselves. They do not merely  take away benefits for non-compliance,
but will pay extra for recipients who do comply with new ob ligations and incentives for
new obligations, because handouts always requir e that. If you believe in true socialism
of taking from people who work hard, to gi ve to people who do not work hard, then
there must be some social obligation, and that obligation is two ways. This sense of give
and take is closer to the kind of human re lationship of which mechanistic welfare has
robbed us. Mechanistic welfare has robbed this  country. But the ultimate dignity that a
person can have is the dignity of work. Wo rk builds self-belief. Work builds self-
esteem. Think about that term self-esteem. It is not other people’s opinion of you but
your opinion of yourself that builds self-esteem.
This bill re-emphasises the importance of work. It re-emphasises the importance of
work for adults, and the importance of working role models for young children and
working role models in the community. It  acknowledges that in many families with
small children both parents work at least part-time. I salute those hard-working families.
We put hard-working families on a pedestal. We  know it is difficult to raise kids and
work around the clock for two-parent familie s struggling to make ends meet. We see
those people as good people, and if we are going to transfer at midnight their hard-
earned taxes by way of a bank transfer to  people who are seeking support from the
Government at a time of need, then there needs to be some obligation to the hard-
working people who are providing the money, otherwise it is called blatant socialism.
Minister Bennett and our coalition partners ar e investing in the social capital of this
country by realigning welfare with the notion of mutual obligation and work. This is
what this bill should have been called: th e “Mutual Obligation of Self-respect and Self-
reliance (and Giving Back Something to th e Community that is Funding the Welfare)
Amendment Bill”.

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: The next one.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: We can call the next one that. We look forward to seeing
further bills and enacting further elements  of our supply agreement in these coming
months. We are turning the co rner in New Zealand. The AC T Party has played a long
role in all of this. We have long argued th at this 40-year experiment in open-ended
welfare has not worked, because it is base d on wrong values. We have argued that a
culture of mutual obligation must replace a culture of entitlement, and this bill is the
arrival of that long march. I am glad to be supporting it as the leader of the ACT Party.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere): Malo le soifua. Thank you for this
opportunity. I rise on behalf of the Labour Pa rty and I want to simply say that the
contribution and presence of Mr Banks after four decades is evidence that the right-
wing ideology of the Jim Bolger Government  failed New Zealand and that the “mother
of all Budgets” of “Ruthless Ruth” during his era failed New Zealand communities. It is
also evident that they have never learnt their lesson.
I would say to this House that the Govern ment’s Social Security (Youth Support and
Work Focus) Amendment Bill is flawed and introduces punitive measures that are
similar to those punitive measures of the decades that Mr Banks hails from, and that are
more characteristic of underdeveloped count ries than of a developed nation such as
ours. Labour opposes this bill because it doe s nothing to address the real issues of
economic growth, productivity, an d employment. It fails to a ddress the barriers that are
faced by New Zealand communities, such as the availability of jobs, such as skills and
19 Jul 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 3767
education, and such as the barriers that sole parents face of child care and the rising cost
of early childhood education.
This debate, if we listen to the numerous submitters who came forward and provided
evidence, is a debate that is important, and it ought to be taken seriously. However, I do
not think that in the period from the first reading to the select committee consideration,
to the second reading, and even throughout the Committee stage the other side has taken
seriously the impact and the ramifications  of the bill and the systems that the
Government is introducing in this bill. I cannot help but be reminded again and again
and again by the substantial submissions made  by significant organisations that service
our community and that deliver and are engaged at the coalface of our communities the
length and breadth of New Zealand. Significa nt organisations such as the Salvation
Army, the Child Poverty Action Group, the women’s organisation, the Human Rights
Commission, the Children’s Commissioner, the Families Commission, all of them
raised concerns and all of them did not s upport the bill that is here. The Salvation
Army—and I remind members on the other side—said succinctly that we are moving
away from the fundamental purpose of the Soci al Security Act of 1964. I want to repeat
it for the sake of this House. The purpose of the Social Security Act, which this bill now
amends, is “(i) to help people to support themselves and their dependants while not in
paid employment; and (ii) to help people to find or retain paid em ployment; and (iii) to
help people for whom work may not curren tly be appropriate because of sickness,
injury, disability, or cari ng responsibilities”—for young children or those who are
elderly or sick—“to support themselves and their dependants:”.
I also want to remind this House that as a developing nation we are a signatory to the
Universal Declaration of Human Rights, a nd, above all, we should be the shining
example in this region of upholding the Univer sal Declaration of Human Rights. I draw
your attention to article 23 of the Univer sal Declaration of Human Rights: “(1)
Everyone has the right to work, to free choi ce of employment, to just and favourable
conditions of work and to protection agains t unemployment. (2) Ev eryone, without any
discrimination, has the right to equal pay for equal work. (3) Everyone who works has
the right to just and favour able remuneration ensuring for himself and his family an
existence worthy of human dignity, and suppl emented, if necessary, by other means of
social protection. (4) Everyone has the righ t to form and join trade unions for the
protection of his interests.” Article 24: “Everyone has the right to rest and leisure,
including reasonable limitation of working h ours and periodic ho lidays with pay.”
Article 25: “(1) Everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate to the health and
well-being of himself and his family, including food, clothing, housing and medical care
and necessary social services, and the right to security in the event of unemployment,
sickness, disability, widowhood, old age or other lack of livelihood in circumstances
beyond his control. (2) Motherhood and chil dhood are entitled to special care and
assistance. All children, whether born in or out of wedlock, shall enjoy the same social
protection.”
I think we have drifted as a country so fa r away from the fundamental principles and
values that we as a country signed up to. We have drifted so far away with this bill from
the fundamental purpose of the Social Security Act 1964, which established our system.
No person I have ever met, no one in my  community, no one in the schools I visit,
whether they be in my electorate or in othe r electorates, ever talk s about how it is their
lifestyle choice to be on a benefit. That is not a lifestyle choice, contrary to what the
other side believes. Jobs, jobs, jobs are what  this Government fails to deliver. I think
that this Government here has mastered the act of appearing to be busy while actually
doing nothing—I have got it wrong—the art of looking busy while achieving nothing,
because so far this Government seems to con cede the fact that it cannot deliver jobs for
3768 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  19 Jul 2012
the country, and is simply sitting on its hands, allowing thousands  and thousands of
New Zealanders to leave our shores for the safety of Australia, for the jobs and the
quality of life that Australia seems to offer them.
As I said, the whole bill is very reminiscent of what Mr Banks’ era delivered, which
we as a country suffered for many, many years.  In fact, in 1999 when Labour came into
power, we were challenged with the high une mployment that National had left this
country with. In 2008 when we left power, un employment was relati vely low, at 3.5
percent. We are now, for women, at 7.1  percent. While 160,000 unemployed New
Zealanders continue to l ook for work, this Government introduces a bill which will
introduce sanctions, or threats, as I have called them, because if they do not do what the
department will force upon them, then they will be faced with sa nctions. My greatest
concern is that, despite the intention the Minister for Social Development had in
drafting this bill, those individuals who will suffer as a consequence—whether
intentional or not—will be children and young people, because when they are 5 years
old, their mum or their dad will be forced to go out to look for work. If they do not find
a job, they will be sanctioned. At 14 years old, that young person will be left at home
because their mum or dad will be forced to go find a job.
I want to say to this Minister that sole mothers do not have a choice. That is not a
lifestyle choice. Sole parents want to be able  to provide for their families and want to
provide for their children, and what this G overnment is doing by introducing sanctions
on sole mothers really is a kick in the guts for them. At the end of the day, it will be the
children who will suffer, and I will point my  finger directly at that Minister, as
responsible.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: The Green Party—

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I think you were busy, but on
two occasions in the last minute the Minister for Social Development used the words “it
is a lie”; one when the memb er was speaking, and one just then. May I ask you to ask
her to withdraw and apologise?

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I have to say I was actually
busy calling the honourable member Jan Logie, but if the member did use that word
then she should withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: I didn’t call him a liar.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: All I can say is that all
members are honourable members; their word  is their bond. If members are found to
have not honoured that, then there are repercussions through the Privileges Committee.

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: I certainly did not ca ll him a liar. What I did say is I felt that
there were lies, but I did not call him a liar, so I did not besmirch the member by calling
him a liar.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Can I thank the Minister for
explaining the situation. Nevertheless we have a rule in this place that no one is called a
liar because indirectly you are not actually calling the pers on that; you are insinuating
that the whole Parliament is like that. So in  that case I would just ask the Minister to
withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: I certainly can withdraw and apologise if that is your ruling.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Thank you—much
appreciated.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: The Green Party, as stated several times already, will oppose the
Social Security (Youth Support and Work Focu s) Amendment Bill. We will continue to
offer alternative solutions, and we hope that  after the next electi on we can be part of
building a society that has a strong foundati on based on a Kiwi sense of a fair go and
community. We have many specifi c concerns about the content of this bill, and many
19 Jul 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 3769
concerns regarding the context within whic h it is operating. We have many concerns
about what we see as some pretty fundament al inconsistencies w ithin this bill, and
many concerns regarding the underlying values inherent in this bill. Ultimately, we have
a different vision for our soci ety and a different view of our fellow New Zealanders. I
would like to speak to that a little bit more.
Last night I went to a presentation by a great organisation called KidsCan, which is
working in New Zealand to provide raincoat s for children who do not have them, shoes
for children who do not have them, and food for children in lower-d ecile schools. This
group is not a political group, it is not advoca ting for structural change, but what it
described is absolutely relevant to our sense of social security and welfare. It described
children who do not know when their birthday is, because their parents have not got
enough money to be able to put on birthday pa rties. It described little girls who are
getting their heads shaved because the cost  of buying lice treatment is half of the
family’s income. It described children who are going to bed in raincoats that were given
to them by this organisation, because they are the warmest thing they own. The people
from this organisation were very clear that it has not met one parent who does not want
the best for their children. Th ey have not met one parent who does not try their hardest
for their children. That is the context we are living in. This is not about poor parenting;
this is about inadequate income. Two out of  five families living in poverty are working
families. Pushing people off welfare into wo rk will not solve the problem of poverty in
this country. What we need to do is increase our base income. This bill does nothing to
achieve social security.
Now to speak a little bit more around the conten t of this bill and the points that we
oppose. We oppose the contracting out of services. The Minister for Social
Development talks about a wraparound servi ce for young people and the need to care. I
absolutely, wholeheartedly suppor t that. I have worked in th e community with a lot of
young people in that situa tion, and I really recognise that when they do not have family
to stand by them, support is important. Ho wever, we cannot support this model when
we are undermining the value and the functioning of the community as opposed to the
State. That is what this bill does. It puts community organisations into the role of the de
facto State. That compromises the ability to build relationships, and undermines the
organisations’ ability to respond to their community needs.
We do not support the starting point of controlling every young person’s finances
and putting them on payment cards. The Soci al Services Committee had very strong
evidence from some young people—and from  young people I spoke to, as well—about
the need for flexibility. In act ual fact, many of their living situations tend to be quite
tenuous, and they need to be able to respond quickly and get out of bad situations. This
provision is not going to help with that problem. In fact, having automatic payments—
things out of their control—may well put them into more precarious situations.
We support aspiration for our young people.  We do not support a one-size-fits-all
solution, which National Certificate of Educational Achievement level 2, as an
aspiration for all young people, is. It is a one-s ize-fits-all solution. It does not recognise
the needs of young people with learning disabili ties. It does not rec ognise the needs of
young people who are refugees who do not ev en have literacy in  their own first
language. It does not follow best teaching practice, which is that you focus on the
students and their learning pattern, not the teachers or some external goal.
We do not support the information-sharing provisions in this bill, which are not
consistent with the Privacy Act. They are an experiment. We actually believe that the
right to privacy goes over, and should go beyond, the Government’s experiment. We
also have concerns that were brought up with us by young women around education.
We really support that model in terms of young women being able to go to schools and
3770 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  19 Jul 2012
have their kids in the same place while they are learning. But we do not have many of
those schools in our country, so the chances  are that a lot of these young women are
going to be sent to courses th at are not going to provide childcare onsite, and they are
going to be separated from their children. There is real potential that that is going to
have an impact on their bonding. We do not believe that that is good for the country.
In terms of the provisions in relation—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: There’s a lot of good bonding going on within the dryer.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: If that member does not think these young women want to bond with
their children, he has obviously not met many  or had many discussions with them. The
DPB—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Well, I’ve got six children; I’ve probably got some idea.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: Are they in that situation? For the DPB, we do not support the work
testing at all, actually. We believe that the evidence supports that when women are
ready to go back to work, and when their children are ready for them to go back to
work, they start looking for work. We do not believe they need to be pushed. We
believe that their individual situations a nd reasons for being on the DPB in the first
place actually often mean they should be ther e with their children, putting their children
first, and, in many cases, healing from what have been some very traumatic experiences,
rather than trying to juggle the needs of their children and juggle the needs of a job,
travel, and life. We believe that that is unrealistic.
I would like to speak to some of the inconsistencies in this bill. One is that the intent,
we are told, of this bill is to take an inve stment approach, a really radical approach. The
Minister has said that she makes no apology fo r the cost of it, that it is going to be
expensive but it will be worth it because it will pay off. Yet the Government used its
financial veto to rule out my Supplementa ry Order Paper, which would have extended
the training incentive allowance to highe r-grade courses, which we know are the
courses that will enable women to get off th e DPB 6 months earlier and enable them to
stay off the DPB for longer. We have got clear evidence on that. The cost of that
provision was only $5 million to $15 million.
I would also like to draw attention to the inconsistency where the Government
purports to want the best for children, yet, ag ain, it used its financial veto against Holly
Walker’s Supplementary Order Paper, wh ich would have provi ded the option for
discretion when officials gauged that sancti oning a parent would make it difficult to
feed, clothe, or care for the well-being of a child. The Government sa id that that would
cost millions of dollars—hundred of millions  of dollars—because it had budgeted for
those sanctions. The needs of the child, obvi ously, do not figure in its considerations.
For us, that is a fundamental inconsistency.
I would also like to talk to some of th e values. The Government talks about the
importance of work, and we also heard th is from the ACT Party. We share that.
Absolutely, work is important. Parenting is work. Actually, contributing to our
community is work. And most people want to wo rk, in paid work or otherwise. Part of
the way we shape our society is by valuing work—not by valuing just the things we say
are work and not valuing what other people cons ider to be work. We would also like to
say that our understanding of a fair go is the understanding that everyone has—that we
give our children a place to start in life that  is comparable, so that they can get ahead
and everyone has the chance of getting ahead in life. We know  that when children are
living in poverty, it means they are going  to have poorer life outcomes, poorer
educational outcomes, poorer employment opportunities—a whole range of really
negative things. This bill is, in fact, entrench ing that inequality in our country, and I do
not believe that inequality is a New Zealand value.
19 Jul 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 3771

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Ahn nyung ha se yo, Mr Speaker . It is a great pleasure
to rise to make a contribution on this th ird reading of the Social Security (Youth
Support and Work Focus) Amendment Bill, but before I go on I would just like to make
a comment about something that Jan Logie ha s spoken about. I cannot  believe that any
good parent would let their child go to bed in  a raincoat because that was the warmest
thing they could possibly find. You can go to an op shop and buy a warm jumper for
50c. You know, I cannot believe that a Gree n member would actually talk about
spending a lot of money on hair lice treatmen t. I mean, you can actually wet the child’s
hair and use a fine-tooth comb to actually get them out. It is called elbow grease. It does
not cost very much. As a mother, I know what that is like.
Over the course of the debates in the passage of this bill I have to say I have become
more convinced how important this bill is. It is exactly where we should be as a nation,
and I commend the fortitude shown throughout the process by the Minister for Social
Development, the Hon Paula Bennett. I also ta ke this opportunity to  thank the officials
for the hard work that they have done in assisting the committee and the members of the
Social Services Committee for their hard work. We have all heard the statistics during
the debates about the number of young people on benefits in this country, and about the
number of young people who leave school who are not employed and are not in training
of any kind whatsoever. We have also heard— and this is something all sides of this
House agree on, I would think—that when pe ople end up on the benefit at a young age,
the likelihood of them staying on the benef it for longer than those who come on to the
benefit later in life is high.
Is this the kind of future that we wa nt for our young people in this country? I
certainly do not, and I am sure that all in this House do not, either, and this bill provides
a way out of the statistics for our young people. The wraparound service for at-risk
youth who otherwise would end up going dow n the path of long-term dependency on
social welfare is what I am passionate a bout, because to me welfare cannot become a
way of life. It cannot go down through the generation of families, and it cannot be an
acceptable way of life. It is purely a safety  net for people who find themselves in
difficult times, to assist them until they get back on their feet again. That was the
intention of social welfare.
During the course of the debate it was a Green member—I think it was Jan Logie—
who said that we needed to go down the pa th of a strength-bas ed approach. I just
wanted to comment that writing off young people as being unable to participate in the
workforce cannot be the strength-based approa ch she is talking about, especially when
members opposite talked about National Certificate of Educational Achievement level 2
being too high a mark for them to achiev e—that these young people could not possibly
meet that goal. I say there is nothing wrong with backing our youngsters to have a goal
and to achieve it.
I want to see a welfare system that does more than just hand out money. I want to see
a welfare system that encour ages young people to aspire to  be great and to do greater
things—to be greater than what they are. I want to see a welf are system that utilises the
expertise of youth support providers who actually know what they are doing in terms of
young people, to wraparound the service and to tell young people that they can do better
and that they are in fact capable. Our we lfare system over many Governments over the
