past has failed our young people. This John Key - led Government is doing something
about it.
Finally, many members opposite have spoken a bout the work-test obligations in the
bill as though they are a punishment for women.  I have to say that at times during the
debate I was made to feel guilty that I am a working mum—a working solo mum of a
13-year-old child. Would it not be fantastic if everyone who had a child could stay at
3772 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  19 Jul 2012
home? I certainly feel guilty when I am not at home due to work commitments and miss
significant events in my son’s life, but it wa s a decision that I made to provide a better
life for my son. It is time fo r all to realise that taxpaye rs should not be  burdened for
lifestyle choices, and I am in no way suggest ing that people choose to be on benefits.
Some do; most do not. But helping people on benefits get out of their situation and to be
work-focused and work-ready is what we ar e doing with this bill, instead of simply
giving them the money and leaving them to it.
This change is long overdue. I commend the Minister for guiding this bill through its
passage through the House. It is a great bill, and I commend it to the House.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR (NZ First) : Talofa lava. Malo le
soifua ma le lagi e mama, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Malo le soifua.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : Fa‘afetai mo le avanoa. Thank you
for the opportunity. Kia ora t ātou katoa. I rise on behalf of the New Zealand First Party
to provide a realistic viewpoint to this debate in the third reading of this so-called Social
Security (Youth Support and Work Focus) Amendment Bill. I am somewhat stunned by
the contributions from John Banks and th e former speaker, and I suggest perhaps
Melissa Lee needs to stick to motorway debates. That is where she can do better.
Let me be real here. There is no que stion surrounding the argument that New
Zealand needs to address the key issue of  welfare reform, or welfare dependency.
However, the bill does not guarantee this. In fact, the only thing it can  guarantee is that
our children, our youth, are being used as guinea pigs in a reform system. This
Government is also too keen to rush in a Trojan Horse, you might call it, which allows
this Government to implement other legisla tion. Perhaps the next one would be a youth
rate. The youth rate will be coming up next at $10.50 or even less.
There is nothing wrong with dreaming a fa ntastic dream, and those who dream do
recognise the importance of dreams that bri ng about positive aspira tions. We all agree
on that. In my previous role as a facilitator for professional development, and, of course,
with the Department of Corrections, I often talked to the participants about dreams and
their relevance to life. I believe that this  bill was meant to be the link between our
youths’ dreams and achieving positive goals in life. After all, the future belongs to those
who believe in the beauty of their dreams.  However, as we all know, although we
acknowledge those who dream of a better future, it is also fair to say that where there is
a dream, there needs to be a vision—because the dreamer can dream the most fantastic
dream, but only a visionary can make that dr eam come true. That is what New Zealand
First believes in.
I do not know about the members on that side  of the House, especially the only ACT
MP, John Banks. From where I sit, this bill is much more suitably called the “Missing in
Action Benefit Bill” or, let me say, the “Missing the Point Benefit Bill”.

items.speaker: Mark Mitchell
items.text: That’s silly.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR: Of course, it is not silly. You should
know that. People up in your electorate, Mr Mark Mitchell, are also in that area. A lot of
them are actually in this category. The Govern ment has failed to put in place a strategic
plan on job creation for those who would be affected by the introduction of this bill. If I
could ask this: are the Minister for Social  Development and the National Government
actually concerned about our yout h, or are they happy to sit back and use the estimated
$520 million funding not for our youth but to  fund the information technology package
to run the reforms? And that is not to mention the additional cost to keep it operating. If
paper shuffling were a job, the Nats would be darn good at it. I ask how we can
guarantee what this Government believes, and I emphasise the word “believes”, because
it means we will rely on the right interpretation for youth.
19 Jul 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 3773
Yes, job training programmes are essential. By the way, can the Government confirm
whether it is receiving funding from the Australian Federal Government for this
Government’s proposed training programmes,  because the Austra lians are certainly
going to be the beneficiary of this bill? Our tertiary students are actually already on a
one-way ticket to Australia. Instead, this Minister is proposing to boost the growing
exodus. The National Government is doing ve ry well as an employment agency for
Australia. We can all recall a former Na tional Government Prime Minister who once
said that New Zealanders who emigrate to Au stralia raise the IQ of  both countries. It is
sad that the Government is pushing this bill  forward. It is a speedy implementation of
legislation in order to avoid close scrutiny, and it deprives ordinary New Zealanders of a
fair opportunity to have their say. The chai rman of the Social Services Committee and
the National members of the committee put forward an unrealistic time frame when
calling for submissions.
Although reducing long-term welfare dependency is something that this Government
needs to address, so must be the schemes to provide realistic solutions for jobs. I can tell
everyone in this House and thos e who are listening to this debate right now what this
bill is a solution to. It is merely a sugar-coating. That  is what this is  all about, and New
Zealand First is concerned about a number of changes proposed in this bill. These
include the use of the private sector to find  jobs, information-sharing provisions within
the bill, the wider welfare reform package, and, of course, the tax to the taxpayers. Why
is that? There is no saving to the taxpayers. At the end of the day, when you look at this
bill, there is absolutely no saving to the ta xpayers. The most appropriate title for this
bill, then, should be the “Political Cronyism Benefit Bill”.
Under this bill the cost to the taxpayers is not only not reduced but the paying out in
administration of the benefit just shifts fr om Work and Income to the Inland Revenue
Department. The bill does not give the opportunity to our youth to learn how to be
independent, and that is the crux of this debate.
Then there is the second phase of this bi ll, which really gets me. The bottom line is
whether this Government will provide jobs  to widowers, to those on the DPB, and
women living alone receiving the benefit. Some  of those people did not have the choice
of becoming solo parents. For some of them  their partners died, for whatever reason,
and so they were put in that position not be cause of their choice but because of the facts
of life.
In respect of the provisi on relating to the use of the National Student Number, we
support that totally. We understa nd the need for that to happ en. We also agree with the
Privacy Commissioner that the changes in th is bill target a group for whom trust in
authority may already be in short supply.
New Zealand First has some serious reserva tions about increases in the use of the
private sector for finding jobs. The goal is to pay private companies or organisations for
every person that comes off the welfare. Th e underlying principle is  fine; we all agree
with the underlying principle. The approach and the implementation of the bill are what
we need the Minister and the Government to  perhaps hear, in terms of what we are
trying to say they need to fix. Women, for as long as we can remember, have always
had an important role in our community. Having a child or becoming a housewife is not
a matter of choice; it is actually a duty. It is a duty for some of our  women. It is a duty
that is willingly accepted by many, and is  in some circumstances compulsory.
Extending work availability expectations and pre-benefit activities to this category is
simply government formed on an impetuous nature. By nature, the Government is again
putting into action privately r un bureaucracy firms. This should not be a shortcut to
creating jobs. This is about getting people off the benefit and into jobs. My challenge to
the Government is to put in place a strategi c plan that will realistically and genuinely
3774 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  19 Jul 2012
provide jobs for our community. Thank you. New Zealand First does not support this
bill.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: This is an important day for our
country, and for our history. It is an especially important day, and a very positive one,
for young people who are at risk of leavi ng school without qualifications, who are
struggling to find work, who are unlikely to acquire a range of vital life skills without
much more active intervention and support, and who are ultima tely in clear danger of
being welfare-dependent, possibly for a lifetim e. That is the reality for far too many
young New Zealanders under existing legislati on and circumstances. That reality is a
tragedy for them, it is a constant worry—or, at least, it cer tainly ought to be—for all
who love and care for them, it is a huge cost to our economy, and it is a major blight on
our society. I am proud to be part of a Government that is determined to tackle this issue
at its core. This is one of the most important and compelli ng issues that made me want
to commit myself to a political career. For me, therefore, this is a very significant day.
I am proud to have played a full part, as a member of the Social Services Committee,
in developing and working on this bill, the Social Security (Youth Support and Work
Focus) Amendment Bill, to the point where its significant provisions are about to be
passed into law. Contrary to the confus ed and dogma-ridden assertions of Opposition
members, this bill is not punitive; it is liberating. This bill does not bash beneficiaries. It
shows very clearly that we belie ve in them, and that we want the very best for them. It
is not heartless and cynical; it is positive an d aspirational. It is a measure that is
desperately needed, and whose time has we ll and truly come. Our Government has
demonstrated this conviction by investing $287.5 million over the next 4 years into
practical support and a range of programmes that will assist New Zealanders out of
welfare and into work.
Our opponents have claimed that they welcom e that principle, but their speeches,
their votes to date, and their intentions as to how they will vote this afternoon show that
they clearly believe the oppos ite. Several Opposition members have worried that young
parents covered by this bill wi ll not have access to childcare.  That is false, and a clear
case of cynical scaremongering, as $80 million was allocated in this year’s Budget for
extra early childhood education childcare places, and those who are the focus of this bill
will enjoy a guaranteed childcare assistance payment. That is because we want the best
not only for those young people but also for their children. For every one of those young
people for whom the intergenerational cycle of welfare dependency can be broken, life
will improve considerably. They will secure the brighter future that this National-led
Government wants for every New Zealander.
Opposition members should support that goal, and endorse these measures to achieve
it. But, instead, they have resorted to dogma and negativity, refusing to acknowledge the
problems, and, instead, saying to those who ar e in this position: “We’re sorry, but for
you, what you have now is as good as it ge ts.” Well, what have those defeatist
merchants of doom told us? Mr Sio seems obs essed with the notion that beneficiaries
will be forced into work, and then will not be  able to live on their wages. Well, if they
move into low-paid work, it is true that fo r a time life will be difficult, and that some
tough choices will be needed.
But that is the reality for them right now, because their income is currently welfare-
dependent. Their financial circumstances may not improve dramatically, but they should
improve. They certainly will not decline. Ov er time, the future for them will be much
brighter. Being back in work will be a bene fit to them, and to those who are dependent
upon them, especially in the longer term. Mr Sio also appears to believe that mothers of
young children who enter paid work are guilty of neglect and bad parenting. Well, that
notion is as ludicrous as it is offensive.
19 Jul 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 3775
Members opposite also bleat repeatedly, as  they have throughout this debate, that
there are no jobs. Well, if that is true in some areas, then nothi ng will change. That is
what the unemployment benefit is for. No one can be forced into  a job that does not
exist. But those who receive the unemploymen t benefit must be prepared to make the
transition when work becomes available to th em. In many cases, that claim simply is
not true. In recent times we have seen that many who have been asked to reapply for the
unemployment benefit have instead cancelled their benefit. More  people than ever
before are currently in work, and many of t hose who were asked to reapply actually did
not do so, because they had already found work or, in some cases, they had gone
overseas. Many vacancies are now advertised and, for reasons that escape many of my
constituents, quite a number of them are never taken up. Nobody is appointed to them.
Many employers, especially those providing  seasonal work, cannot attract workers.
Sometimes the issue is not the absence of a j ob but a reluctance to take it, and that, too,
must change.
I salute the hard work of our Minister for Social Development, Paula Bennett, and
thank her, on behalf of all New Zealanders  who want to get ahead in life, for her
courage and determination in facing up to this challenge and for steering this bill
through to its expected enactment today. I acknowledge Peseta Sa m Lotu-Iiga and my
colleagues on the Social Services Committee. We have worked hard on this bill. On this
side of the House we care passionately a bout the issue and all who are trapped in
welfare dependency. We want so much more for them, and this bill contains vital
measures to help them to break the cycle and to fulfil their potential. I am proud to have
played my part in progressing this bill. I am  happy to be held accountable for it, and to
be judged on its success. That is how conf ident I am that this bill will achieve its
objectives.
I have always argued in favour of a welfare system for New Zealand that responds as
generously and as compassionately as possibl e to the many thousands of people of all
ages who need that support. Many of them have been dea lt one cruel blow in life after
another. Their stories are ofte n distressing, and it is our collective obligation to assist
them. How privileged we are to be able to do that. That is what Michael Joseph Savage
and his colleagues had in mind back in 1935, and perhaps even Richard John Seddon
and others before them. But welfare has got  out of hand, and now penalises and traps
many of those whom it ought to liberate.
This bill is an important step in refocu sing the system and gett ing our beneficiaries
back on track. That cannot happen soon enough. I encourage everyone in that position
to embrace the opportunities th at this bill presents to them, and I offer them the
assurance that this Government believes in them and backs them to the hilt. Kia kaha.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: I wish I could say it is a pleasure to take my last
call on this bill, the Social Security (Youth Support and Wo rk Focus) Amendment Bill,
but I do not think it is a pleasur e. In fact, it is with some sadness that I get to speak on
this particular bill in its third reading.
From the time that this bill has been in the House, we have looked for some kind of
logic that it was trying to present that we c ould agree with and that  we could relate to,
and that could relate also to the reality of  what we find out there. We searched, we
examined, and we listened very carefully to the thinking of those who are experts, by
anybody’s calculation, who presented to the Social Services Committee. They were
people who have researched this field, who work in this field every day, and who came
to the select committee with a lot of thinking and a lot of experience behind them, to tell
us what they saw in this bill and what the gap was be tween what ought to happen and
what was being provided in this bill. What we found was a big gap between all the
factors that needed to be taken into account  to make life better for our children, for our
3776 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  19 Jul 2012
mums, and for our families, and what the provisions of this bill provide. For us, there
was a real disconnect between what the Government has said it is trying to do, and what
this bill will produce from our perspective.
Government members are convinced that th ese are the only provisions that will
reduce welfare numbers, and this has been their driving goal throughout this—what will
reduce welfare numbers. Those who submitted told us that they are wrong—that they
are absolutely wrong. Yes, we did work hard  at the Social Services Committee and I
wish we had worked hard to understand what they were telling us as well. In fact, in my
view, members of the select committee from  the Government side have actually not
argued their points with any ri gour, particularly in the th ird reading debate where we
went clause by clause. The rigour was not there.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: We’re in the third reading debate.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: It was left time and time again, Mr Macindoe—time and time
again it was left to the Minister for Social Development to take call after call from the
chair and simply explain the same logic, the same things that will happen. There will be
wraparound services, this will be great, etc. That happened time and time again.
Members obviously were not that convinced. Th ey were very ready to clap when the
Minister gave one of her 5 or 10-minute renditions from the chair during the Committee
stage, but certainly they did not expand rigorously thei r arguments. They were not
convincing.
But let us be clear. Labour believes, and th is side of the House believes, passionately
in investment—in actually investing in t hose who are likely to be caught and who are
likely to find themselves on their own, cari ng for young children or adolescents for that
matter. We agree that we ought to invest in  that particular group. We would invest in
helping young people prepare much better for their adult lives and their early adult
lives. We would provide sole parents with  real opportunities to prepare for work
through programmes like the training incentive allowance, which the other side does not
believe in. We know they work, because they worked for the Minister herself. She is
our best case in point, if you like. But that  is all gone, and what we now find—what the
Government members put in place of that—is the rhetoric of investment. The rhetoric of
investment is hollow, because it somehow takes a word that has positive connotations
and imposes that on the logic of this bill, trying to make it good.

items.speaker: It is quite interesting
items.text: when Labour spends  money on social services and on welfare,
then it is welfare dependency; when the Government spends money, then it is
investment. That is intellectually dishonest. It is quite amazing that Tim Macindoe gets
up and talks about this side of the House be ing dogmatic, in terms of dogma. Well, that
is exactly what that member  is doing, and that is exactly what the Government is—
absolutely dogmatic. And it is absolutely unfounded by research a nd by anything else.
Dogma does not need that kind of logic. I thought this Government was going to use
research that was evidence based and evidence led. Well, it is not.
We have said throughout this debate that the Government is focused only on getting
people off welfare, and it seems that it is  at any cost—and it is at any cost. The
Government denies this, but this is its only motive. The Government tries to mask this
in the language I have talked about—the lang uage of investment, etc., and the language
of wraparound services. Who argues against wraparound services? Of course we should
have wraparound services; that should be there now. There is nothing radical about that.
But the Government has not given us the logi c of how that is goi ng to be done. What it
really has done is it has really been narrow in its analysis. For one member it was that
these young women have made a lifestyle ch oice. For another it  is about hope and
ambition. For another it is just a new system. What is it? Why do the members opposite
and the Government not get their way round ? My friend and colleague Mr Macindoe
19 Jul 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 3777
tells me he came to the House just for this purpose. I want  to ask Mr Macindoe why he
bothered. If this was to be his finest hour , why did he bother? Because I do not think
this is going to do that. Of course, for the Minister it is a bit like the cavalry. She said
“Change is on its way.”—the cavalry is coming.
When we examine the arguments the members opposite have presented, we have
exposed all of them. They say th at work is the best way; th erefore, we must have work
testing. Well, of course work and creating work is the best response to welfare; we have
heard enough about that. But th is is not what they have been saying. There is no real
plan to create that work, only a concession that if there is no  work there, then this will
not apply. Why bother? Why do we not focu s on wraparound services? Why do we not
focus on getting those who are on benefits in the best place possible to enter the
workforce? This is what the previous programme did, which is what the Minister herself
is the beneficiary of—and good on her. I have congratulated her in other speeches on
taking the opportunities that were made av ailable then and finding her way through.
And why do we now pull the ladder for others? It seems as if this whole bill and this
whole area of welfare reform is designed to  pacify a group of their constituency who
really believe that the problems of New Ze aland can be traced to  those who are on
welfare, and if we did not have that, then everything else would be fine.
It is the same when we get to their ar guments about parenting. This is an anti-
parenting bill. A mother of a 1-year-old now has to be work tested, and if there is a 5-
year-old as well, then that mother will not have the time that she needs to care for the
child.

items.speaker: Hon Amy Adams
items.text: Rubbish!

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: It is in the bill, Amy Adams. That is in the bill. Read the bill,
Minister, because that is in the bill. That  is the argument. I wonder whether members
opposite and members of the Cabinet really under stand what this bill is about. They are
saying that for a mother with  a 14-year-old, under this G overnment, the 14-year-old is
on their own—I say to that member. They are on their own because there will be no
protection if their mother happens to be a welfare beneficiary. That is what this
Government has produced, and yet we know from all the evidence that that young age
and that older age are exactly when the cari ng abilities of the parents are needed for
those children.
This side is passionate about this bill, b ecause this Government is destroying family
life. It pretends to be family orientated, but  it is destroying family life. There is a bill
next week that will do it as well. We will ar gue the same argument next week. That is
what this Government is doing. Then it brin gs on people like John Banks, who tells us
in his sycophantic way that this is the be st thing since sliced bread. When did John
Banks become relevant to this Parliament? All he has done is make inane calls on points
of order about somebody using a particular word. There is just so much wrong about
this bill. From the get-go to the closedown now , we have argued consis tently that it is
bad. We have also looked to see what coul d be salvaged, and there is not much. Thank
you.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Can I just make it quite clear to the
members on the other side that this part y—and actually most New Zealanders—values
working mothers. If you are working, it does not mean that you are letting your children
down. We back them, and fundamentally that  is what these members’ argument has
been about—they are not prepared to back the people whom this party will.
Before I go on I just want to commend the Minister for Social Development on this
bill, the Social Security (Youth Support and Work Focus) Amendment Bill, for the hard
work, the compassion, and the enthusiasm that  she has shown with it. I also want to
extend thanks to Mr Lotu-Iiga, the chairperson of the Social Services Committee, for his
3778 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  19 Jul 2012
chairmanship, and also thank fellow members on the committee from across the
political spectrum. I have enjoyed the experience of working on this bill. I think it is fair
to say that we do not always agree on things —and that is healthy—but I think it is also
fair to say that we all do very much care about this particular issue for New Zealanders.
Su’a William Sio: You’re such a greaser, Mike.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Yes, I have often been called that.
The core focus of this bill is really around young people and the manner in which we
can support them, because the reality for thousands of young people—young
teenagers—who are currently in that pipeline is  that they are starin g down the barrel of
a collision with an adult benefit, and, certainly, experience tells us that they will be there
for a very, very long time.
Like all of us, these young people have dreams, hopes and aspirations, and often
through no fault of their own they find themselv es in very challeng ing situations where
they will struggle to achieve those things. It does not mean they do not have those
dreams. The challenge for the community—indeed, the challenge for us as legislators—
is to actually find ways to address that is sue. The burgeoning problem with welfare is
something that has concerned not only New Zealanders but everyone in this House and
this political spectrum for many years,  as $22 million a day is not financially
sustainable, but, more important, the human cost, the human collateral, is substantial.
At the core of this bill we  are looking at three major pl anks. The first is a stronger
work focus. The focus is about enabling these young people to find their way into work.
We have heard much from the other side abou t the fact that there is no work, which I
find amusing when the Opposition will rail ag ainst every single policy and every single
bill that this Government has put forward to grow the economy. So if they were genuine
about supporting work growth  and job creation, then they might find themselves
supporting what we are trying to do to grow this economy in very challenging times.
This bill also provides a mechanism to build capacity for work in these young
people. It is a major cultural shift in the way that we have addressed welfare in the past.
A very good example of that is the incentive payments that form part of this bill.
Sanctions have long been a part of the Soci al Security Act, but incentives providing
encouragement and promoting behaviour by way of financial incentives is something
new and, I think, something we have not spent enough time focusing on.
Beyond that, the payment card and the assist ed management of essential bills, I
think, will provide a number of these young people with an opportunity to step back
from the stress that their lives are under a nd focus on what we want them to do—to be
able to get control in their lives again, to be able to develop the skill sets that will match
them with employers, who I know want them . Certainly, in my electorate they are
saying to me “We will employ these young people. We just want them to come here and
show us they are prepared to work and prepared to learn.”
I believe that this suite of changes will ma ke a huge difference in the lives of these
very challenged young people who are at a very difficult stage in their life,
notwithstanding their circumst ances. The other important th ing is the monitoring and
guidance that the youth support providers will give  these young people. I think this is
very important. For many, it will fill a gap that is lacking in their own family.
Changes for teen parents are, again, anothe r very, very important focus of this bill.
The work focus must be there with them, the same as it is with other people on welfare,
because they also will have dreams, wants,  hopes, and aspirations. When the work is
suitable, and when they reach an age wher e their youngest children are 5 or 14, or their
second and subsequent child is 1, then we expect them to be  available for work, and we
will support them with childcare to ensure  that. Being in work does not impede a
mother’s relationship with he r child; if anything, it will enhance it. It provides a
19 Jul 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 3779
platform for far greater choices for that mo ther, and a sense of pride and something in
her day that she otherwise would not get while she is sitting at home waiting for crumbs
from the State.
This bill is the first step in fundamentally  changing a culture that, I believe, has been
very disabling for people on welfare for some time. This is about enabling. This is about
supporting. It is not about ju st giving them money and l eaving it up to them. You can
give a little dollar here, and an extra one here or there, but ultimately that has not
worked and this bill is about doing what will work: providing management, incentives,
and support, and preparing them for the world of opportunity and the world of work that
actually they should be in, they should want to  be in, and we certainly want them to be
in.
This bill goes where the O pposition parties certainly w ould not, and certainly not
over in the Greens, that is for sure. This bill is about investing in and backing young
people, believing in them to have a drea m and actually backing them to get on and
achieve it, and ensuring that we have got  the right balance be tween obligations and
responsibilities. And we should not forget th at—it is about achieving the right balance.
What is the reward for the young people? The reward, in my view, is a little more than
just being prepared to be, and actually bei ng, in work. It is actually about having a
purpose. I think it is about having opportunitie s. I think it is about having self-esteem
and a sense of self-respect in oneself, and we all get that wh en we feel as if we have
done something to contribute to the world each day.
This bill is the first step in the long overdue changes th at New Zealanders want and
need. The Opposition will oppose it, but we have come to expect that from them. Deep
down I suspect that they quite ag ree with a number of these changes. It is just that this
Government got on with doing what has needed  to happen. We are wa lkers, not talkers.
I want to commend the Minister once agai n for the work that she has done, and I
wholeheartedly commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I understand that the next call is a
split call.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: I can assure the member opposite that,
deep down, nowhere does Labour secretly agr ee with the measures in this bill, the
Social Security (Youth Support and Work Fo cus) Amendment Bill. I am happy to stand
here and take my final call as part of a Labour team that has consistently opposed the
reforms in this bill. Labour believes that we  need a set of mechanisms that will address
the barriers to getting people off welfar e and into work. Those barriers are the
availability of work. Another one of those ba rriers is the availability of childcare, and
quality and affordable childcare. And the thir d barrier is the issue of skills and whether
people on benefits have the requisite skills to get back into the paid workforce.
Let us first of all briefly look at the issu e of the availability of work. Throughout the
passage of this legislation, members oppos ite have tried to appease their own
conscience by hailing to the maker of the we lfare State, Mickey Savage, and somehow
making themselves sleep at night by sayi ng Michael Joseph Savage would approve.
Well, what they are doing is a whole lot more Margaret Thatcher than Mickey Savage.
That lady is not for turning when it comes to these welfare reforms. Michael Joseph
Savage believed in a social security system where there were a set of rights and a set of
obligations for those on welfar e, but there were also right s and obligations on the State
to create jobs for people—that an active St ate and an active Government did not leave
its citizens to languish in the way this Government is prepared to do.
New Zealanders want to work. The househol d labour force survey tells us that. We
saw that when Labour came into power in 1999 it faced an unemployment queue of
162,000. When Labour left office in 2008 there were 17,700 on the unemployment
3780 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  19 Jul 2012
benefit. This had not been achieved by punitive measures; this had been achieved by
economic development and the creation of j obs. We did not just muck around, playing
around with cycleways; we actually created jobs.
But the issue that I really want to fo cus on today is the issue of young people and
skills training. We are told that this legisla tion introduces all kinds of incentives to get
young people back to work. There are all kinds of financial carrots and financial sticks,
so there are punitive measures if they do not turn up for training. I want a National
member to take a call and to tell me why th ey voted against my amendment to this bill,
which actually offered an opportunity for real  jobs matched with real skills training.
Why is it that National would not match up the opportunity, the genuine and real
opportunity we have to train our young pe ople to be active in  the rebuild of
Christchurch? Why would they not explicitly  put the opportunities that are going, that
are languishing and are not being taken up, in  terms of the $42 million that is being
allocated for the rebuild of Christchurch in  skills training? Why did they vote against
this? It is because this legislation is not hing but a dog whistle to their constituency.
They are more interested in punitive measur es, rather than real  opportunities for our
young people—real opportunities matched with real  jobs that will offer them a lifetime
of employment. But, no, what we can talk a bout is “building capacity for work”, and
other rhetoric like “work focus”, like the me mber we just heard from. How about just
plain, old-fashioned apprenticeship skills traini ng and then going into a job? This is not
something that members opposite believe i n. This is not something that members
opposite are willing to vote for, and it is certainly not some thing that this legislation
does anything to achieve.
This set of measures, this so-called we lfare reform, does nothing to address the
underlying causes of why peopl e are on benefits. Member s opposite cannot sleep at
night by telling themselves, repeating over and over, that Michael Joseph Savage would
approve. He would not. They have failed to address the core reason of welfare
dependency in this country.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: T ēnā koutou. The Social Security (Youth
Support and Work Focus) Amendment Bill is  the unlovely love child of the Welfare
Working Group and the National-ACT Government. It is a polite description to call it
misguided. I would like to go back to Mi chael Joseph Savage and the 1964 original
Social Security Act, which emerged from th e realisation that some people at some time
in their lives need State support.  Statistics make it very clea r that it is often for a matter
of months rather than years, so I am not sure what this beat-up is all about.
It is clear that the original Act recognised terms that we might now find archaic, like
“woman alone”, “disabled”, and “invalids  benefit”. Some of those names are
disempowering in contemporary terms, but wh at was behind them was the recognition
that the State has a role in supporting peopl e who are sick, who are caring for children,
or who are caring for other peopl e, and that that is actually a valid thing to do. In the
case of a woman alone, it was a recognition, wh ich is now denied by this bill, that, in
fact, women who care for others end up on less income when they are older. A simple
fact of pay inequity and the voluntary work they do often means they  have less money.
That benefit is gone. There is  no guilt if you are a working parent, but, equally, there is
no guilt if your work is at home. So let us forget about guilt and ge t real about what is
going on for parents.
What was proposed in the original Ac t sounds like common sense, decency, and
human dignity, and it is especially true in a recession, when our society has become one
of the most unequal in the OE CD. The Government says, and I have heard it a lot this
afternoon, that it wants to help people on  benefits—I think the word used was
“liberation”, which was kind of ironic—by gi ving tax cuts to the top 10 percent and
19 Jul 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 3781
then sanctioning the poorest peop le. I find that term “liberati on” rather fascinating. It is
a little bit like the George Orwellian quote that the louder you make it, the bigger the
lie. However, I would like to go back to the work of my own colleagues, who have done
a great job on this bill.
I would like to go back to the work of Holly Walker and her Supplementary Order
Paper on the need for a child impact assessm ent. What Holly was talking about was the
need to recognise that this entire bill impacts on children, and that if a thorough
assessment had been done on that impact, it would be a very different bill. It would be a
very different bill if it was a child-centred bill, and if it was goi ng to recognise that
existing poverty should never be exacerbated for our children. The Government’s
decision to veto our amendment to give Work  and Income the discretion not to apply a
sanction if it was detrimental to child well-being is effectively an admission of how
harmful this bill will be to children. It is shocking that the Government is already
banking on the savings of hundreds of millions  of dollars by imposing sanctions, and it
shows you what the attitude of Work and Income staff will be when deciding whether to
sanction or not. The Government has already banked the kids’ lunch money.
It is also really, really disappointing to see that the Government would not support
Jan Logie’s amendment. A drop in the buc ket of $5 million to $15 million would have
made a huge difference. The mother’s educatio n, as we know from the evidence, is the
best predictor of the child’s outcome. So if you want children to thrive, you support
their mothers to get an edu cation. You also make sure ch ildren have access to their
parents, rather than making sure their parent s are out being work te sted or walking the
streets looking for jobs. They need their pa rents to be around. Here is the opportunity
for the Government to talk about an investment approach. However, it has failed.
During every recession there is a tiresome  and damaging beat-up, and it is always
beneficiaries. No one pretends that livi ng on a benefit is easy, even in the good times.
The Green Party believes in job creation a nd educational opportunity, not work testing
for non-jobs and cuts to what is  currently a pittance. What saddens me about this bill is
that children, women, disabled people, an d others who are under attack and can be
sanctioned cannot actually fight back. They  cannot get up and say: “We are decent
people who would love the dignity of work when it’s workable, not the stigma and
sanction that the powerful will now take their opportunity to impose upon us.”
The bill is unworkable in parts of the country. Work and Income already knows that
it is unworkable, so, really, th e whole thing is what I woul d call a giant non-step in the
wrong direction. It is a fiasco. Thank you.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I am proud to take the final call on the Social
Security (Youth Support and Work Focus) Amendment Bill. There has been a lot of talk
about evidence. It is not hard  to realise that you do not ne ed a lot of ev idence to know
that the longer people are on a benefit, the mo re harmful it is not only for them but also
for their family, their community, and the country as a whole. There is enough evidence
that says that if you go on younger, you stay on longer.
The key aspect of this bill is the word “focus”. There has been a lot of talk about
where the jobs are. This bill is not about jobs, because that would be about numbers and
outputs. This bill is about outcomes. Yes,  the numbers are important, because they
indicate change, but the most important thin g this bill is focu sed on is improving
outcomes. This is the difference, because it changes the words and reframes them in a
way that gives it a sense of vision. Previ ously, in the welfare system everything was
worded with the word “benefit”. What this bill is doing is chan ging that and using
words such as “future focus”, “youth suppor t”, and “work focus”. What that tells us,
and tells people who enter into support that is  absolutely needed at a time of need, is
that while they are there there is an opportun ity for reprieve, but th at at the same time
3782 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  19 Jul 2012
they should not lose sight of the hope they have to achieve their dreams and their
vision—hence the reason for the term “Futur e Focus”. That is th e difference we are
making.
We have been accused of many things. In f act, people have used the words “benefit
bashing”. I think the only people who have  been bashed around are the members on
either side of the House. Also, there has b een a little bit of drama. I think there have
been drama classes in some of the caucuses across the way. We have heard words such
as “genocide”. We have heard words such as  “putting the boot into  beneficiaries”, and
that could not be further from the truth. We  have had accusations and finger-pointing at
the Minister for Social Deve lopment herself and even at other members who have been
here. It was highly offensive when Mr Pr asad assumed that young mothers and mothers
would not have the sense of wanting to be a working mother—to have their children and
work at the same time. It was offensive to members on this side of the House, and I
imagine it was offensive to many, many women in our communities.
This bill is the first stage in welfare reform. I just want to tell the other members that
there is much more to come. So the Ginsu knives are coming. The Opposition will have
you believe that people will be forced into work. This is not true. The expectation is that
people will be available to work. Let me just say that word again—available. You see, it
is a future focus. It is about being available for work. There will be no sanction, and that
is fair and reasonable. The bulk of people affected by this bill are young people, and the
focus is on training and education. This is a stepping stone. I will repeat it again so that
the Opposition members understand: this bi ll is a stepping stone. Why? Because
evidence shows that when you go on a benef it younger, you stay on it for longer. The
providers that will be there to provide support are called—and here is another key
word—navigators. They are not enforcers of th e law or of a system; they are navigators
to help our young people find the opportunities that are there.
This is an active system, not an inactive system. Here is the interesting thing, because
a previous speaker, Ms Woods, asked “Where are the jobs?”. Let me just tell you this. If
that was right, if there were a plethora of jobs available under the current system, which
were there under the Labour Government, th ere were no obligations. People did not
have to look for a j ob, and 79 percent of those on a bene fit prior to Future Focus being
implemented had no obligations  to seek work. This is an  active system. This system
provides greater flexibi lity. It introduces greater flexibil ity into the hours of work for
part-time work and full-time work. Tests fo r beneficiaries are subject to work-test
obligations. This is not a mean-spirited bill . All it does is extend the opportunities that
are there.
This bill also authorises information sharing.  It authorises information to be shared
between the Minister of Education and the Mi nister for Social Development in order to
allow the provision of services to young people, between the provider and the
organisations. Why are we focusing on young people? Again, because we know that
when you enter into the system younger, you stay in it for longer.
This bill is also about educational benchmarks. What concerned us was that on the
other side of the House there was the dumbing  down of expectations . It was said that
NCEA level 2 was a bridge too far. [ Interruption] It was a bridge t oo far. We are not
about that. We are about setting educatio nal benchmarks, because you see, Ms Woods,
Mr Prasad, surely you would know that you w ould not set those expectations for your
children. What right do you have to set expectations lower than those you would have
for your own children? Under this bill, this Government sets out the same expectations
that we have for our children. It increase s work expectations. Again, prior to the
National Government’s Future Focus changes, 79 percent of beneficiaries had no work-
19 Jul 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 3783
test obligations. This figure is now 64 percen t, and with the implementation of this bill
we believe it will decrease to 60 percent.
My final words are these. Many members over there have asked us how we will
sleep, and I end with this: all of us who co me into this House and have the opportunity
to make a change, do so with a conscience. We have to, because one day we will all be
held accountable for that which we have s upported. I support this bill; we support this
bill. It is a bill that give s a sense of vision. It creates a sense of focus. It creates
flexibility. It sets a benchmar k of expectation that we all have for all our children. This
is a bill of opportunity, and we will see the results and the outcomes that will truly make
a difference to the young people of our country. Thank you.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Social Security (Youth Support
and Work Focus) Amendment Bill be now read a third time.
Ayes 64
New Zealand National 59; Māori Party 3; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Noes 57
