Part 1  Amendments to Biosecurity Act 1993 (continued)
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labou r—West Coast - Tasman) : I will take an
opportunity to lead in again on Part 1, which is basically the big part of the Biosecurity
Law Reform Bill—the significant part of it. It sets up requirements around pest-
management strategies, which are the plans, I guess, to get rid of or manage diseases
that are already here, such as tuberculosis. St rategies for others will be developed. Ones
around rabbit calicivirus disease, or the rabbi t as a pest, hopefully will be developed
further down the track.
Can I say on behalf of my electorate, in part icular, that one of the obligations in this
bill that I have to endorse and applaud the Government for is the good neighbour
obligation in here. It does place upon the Crow n, as the neighbour of many farmers and
private property owners, an obligation to  engage with them  through these pest-
management strategies and to be a participan t, just like every other private farmer and
landowner. I applaud that initiative.
At the same time, I have to go back and al ert anyone who might be listening to this
debate to the fact that although Labour sup ports this bill, we have some serious
questions. In regard to the Government-indus try agreements, what I must point to—and
there will be a lot of people out there who have  not read the report—is the review of the
import requirements and the border process in light of the entry of Pseudomonas
syringae pv. Actinidiae into New Zealand. One of th e recommendations in that—and I
hope it is not taken up—is that the Ministry for Primary Industries needs to look at the
relative cost-benefit ratios of reprioritisi ng its resources towards managing risks for
economically significant industries. One of the concerns of the small sector groups—the
likes of hothouse growers; pipfruit is not  a small one, but summer fruit is, and
avocados—is that they do not think that  under the Government -industry agreements
they will get a fair go and an opportunity for them to negotiate an affordable deal to
manage any risk incursion or, in fact, to have  input into the preventive measures at the
3784 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 19 Jul 2012
border. The point being that here is a r ecommendation that points to the insufficient
resourcing in biosecurity and says: “Well, if you do not have money, reprioritise and
forget about the small sectors.” That is effectively what it says.
There may well be net benefits  in reprioritising the Ministry for Primary Industries’
resources away from smaller, less strategic industries in order to ensure the risks to
high-value sectors are appropriately managed. What that says is that we will put the
resources into dairy, kiwifruit, pipfruit, and meat and we will forget about the rest. Well,
those sectors need to be well aware of th e dangers. Under the current Government’s
management of biosecurity, ther e is insufficient resource to have a proper system, and
the shifting around of those resources may very well mean that they miss out.
The recent incursion of fruit fly is a classic example. I gu ess it would have been the
whole fruit sector engaged under an MIA— a GIA, sorry; I am getting my MIAs and
GIAs confused here, as it is not the Meat  Industry Association but a Government-
industry agreement—then I am not sure how  we would engage. Thankfully, there was
quick action on that—the one fly—at a cost of $1.4 million. That issue was addressed.
We did not have a wider spread of the Qu eensland fruit fly, thankfully. But you have
got sectors here like summer fruit that ar e crying out for the ministry to X-ray all
incoming baggage into the country, because so mehow that larva got into this country
and we did not pick it up at the border.
There are hundreds of thousands of containe rs coming into this country every year
and they are not checked. There are hundreds of  thousands of visitors coming into this
country each year and they are not checked. Direct exit means that those people go out
without any physical check whatsoever. The vague hope, the vain hope, that the dogs
are around to check it out, in fact, does not apply to Wellington—has not applied since
October last year—and there have been se rious shortages of dogs around the ports and
airports of this country for some time. I understand that the ministry might be upping it
by four in Auckland, but we have a serious—

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I rise on behalf of th e New Zealand First Party.
We are opposed to the passage of this bill , the Biosecurity Law Reform Bill, in its
present form. New Zealand First is strongly committed to the promotion and
preservation of New Zealand’s biosecurity. We understand that the intention of this bill
is to enhance and improve the level of that  biosecurity, and we support the amendments
that it will bring to severa l other pieces of legislation, namely the Maritime Transport
Act 1994, the Ombudsmen Act 1975, the Wild Animal Control Act 1977, and the
Wildlife Act 1953. We see the br inging together of relevant  legislation under a single
umbrella as being a positive move in terms of the imposition and enforcement of
measures intended to safeguard the biosecur ity of New Zealand, which is undeniably of
crucial importance to our ag riculture and to tourism, a nd thereby to our economy and
way of life.
We acknowledge the work done by the pr evious Primary Production Committee and
appreciate the lengths and detail to which that committee went in order to ensure that
what has been presented to the House is a far more workable bill than that which the
committee originally found itself tasked wi th examining. Indeed, in reading the
Hansard from the previous Parliament, it is ap parent that members from both sides of
the House found immediate and obvious faults in  the bill as it ha d been prepared. The
committee made nine substantive changes and recommendations to the Government, all
of which were accepted.
From this I am given cause not only to be reassured as to the commitment of the
committee to achieving workable and practical  outcomes, but also to wonder why and
how such an important piece of legislation could have been so flawed to begin with. It is
this inherently flawed nature of the constr uction and, more important , the focus of this
19 Jul 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 3785
bill that forms the basis of the New Zealand First Party’s opposition to it, rather than the
detail of its application, wh ich has already been addressed.  In addition, given the bill’s
focus, as we see it, combined with the c oncurrent adoption of cer tain new technologies
and existing budget-driven contemporary practices at the border, it is our view that these
elements will in fact work t ogether, in our estimation, not to strengthen New Zealand’s
biosecurity but, indeed, to weaken it.
There are five key areas identified in th is bill: border risk management, marine
biosecurity, readiness and response, pest management, and compliance and
enforcement. In terms of marine biosecurity, the New Zealand First Party is encouraged
by the inclusion of the 200-mile exclusive eco nomic zone within the boundaries of the
bill’s jurisdiction. We believe that this will enhance the safety of the existing fishery, as
well as contributing to the minimisation of ot her risks associated with sea traffic, and
further risks with a potential to impact  on the New Zealand mainland and major
outlying islands from other marine-based ac tivities, including those associated with
offshore mining and oil exploration.
We are pleased also that the bill facilitates the implementation of the International
Convention for the Control and Management of Ships’ Ballast Water and Sediments
2004. This convention aims to minimise the pot entially negative or deleterious effects
of ballast water carried by cargo ships, generally collected in or near the coastal waters
of one port and discharged at the next , and often including real and possible
contaminants, such as biological material s including plants, animals, viruses, and
bacteria. These materials can include non-na tive species, which may impact on aquatic
and marine ecosystems, causing a variety of  negative effects, ranging from civil
nuisance value through to serious ecological and economic damage.
Likewise, New Zealand First welcomes the provisions in this bill that enable a
national policy direction to be formulated a nd imposed with regard to pest management
and control. New Zealand First believes that a collective st rategy coordinated by
Government will enable all individuals and ag encies involved in, or responsible for, the
control, destruction, or other management of  existing and potential pests to work to a
known standard in the formation of thei r operational plans and methodologies. We
believe that this will greatly assist in the eradication or effective control of pests that
may exist, or cross between, regional and jurisdictional boundaries.
We are also pleased that the Crown as a landowner will be included in regional pest-
management rules under the provisions of th e bill, correcting what we see as the
anomaly of its present exclus ion. Land not curren tly required to meet regional pest-
management rules includes not only that ma naged by the Department of Conservation
and Land Information New Zealand, but also that controlled by the Defence Force, the
Department of Corrections, the Ministry of  Education, the Ministry of Justice, the
Crown Forestry Group, and the New Zealand Transport Agency.
So there are good things in the bill, and the stated intent is a good one, with which
we agree. As I have said, we acknowledge the good work that the previous committee
has done on a cross-party basis towards bringing the provisions of this bill into line with
that stated intention. However, where New Zeal and First sees the bill as failing is in its
approach to the remaining provisions not yet addressed—those of border risk
management, readiness and response, and co mpliance and enforcement. We appreciate
that the aim of the bill’s authors is to include some carrot along with the stick, to reward
those who have a good track record w ith regards to upholding and improving
biosecurity, as well as punishing those whose record of performance is poor.
But it is in the relaxation of inspection-base d activities and the change in focus away
from direct and intensive governmental invol vement in the process of ascertaining the
presence of risk factors and or ganisms, which is an essentia l element of the reward side
3786 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 19 Jul 2012
of the equation, that in our view places the bi osecurity of New Zealand at greater rather
than lesser risk. I note from the se cond reading of the bill that the Hansard contains
references of concern from some Oppos ition MPs that the move towards greater
industry self-regulation may be driven by a de sire to ease and accele rate the movement
of goods, in line with the requirements of th e World Trade Organization. Be that as it
may, it is of great concern to the New Zeal and First Party that removing the direct
involvement of inspection and enforcement of regulations for any industry, coupled
with an increase in penalties for those subsequently found to be in breach of them, is not
a formula that has proven to be successful in New Zealand in recent years. It is
somewhat akin to putting an ambulance at the bottom of the cliff rather than a fence at
the top.
I would suggest to members that both lea ky homes and Pike River came about under
regulatory regimes that had been relaxed in  a similar manner. Although a desire to
speed the process of importation and intern ational travel for those who have not
transgressed against the requirements of the border may be of honourable intent, we are
acutely aware that our primarily agrarian  economy is but one mistake away from
disaster. The most careful of frequent trav ellers could very easil y bring in a threat,
inadvertently and unintentionally, the conseque nces of which have the potential to be
dire for the nation as a whole.
We have seen the effects of the Pseudomonas syringae pv. Actinidiae disease on our
kiwifruit industry and the varroa mite on th e bee-keeping and honey industries. And, of
course, we all know that New Zealand lives with the constant spectre of foot-and-mouth
disease, the repercussions of which have thankfully yet to be visited upon us. I can tell
this House that the root viru s phylloxera arrived in Central Otago during my time in the
wine industry there, and that was with all the necessary protocols in place around
movement. Without them, it would doubtless have  made its appearance decades earlier,
and had it done so, it is doubtful the New Z ealand’s reputation as the producer of the
world’s finest Pinot noir could ever have been established.
A piece of fruit or a jar of  honey accidentally left in the luggage of a business
traveller with a hitherto unbl emished record could have c onsequences for this country
that no fine or monetary penalty could possibl y hope to address. Similarly, an insect or
animal pest slipping through the net of an importer with previously impeccable systems
and credentials could likewise impact on the nation beyond th e ability of any
punishment to deter, particularly when any such transgression is likely to be entirely
unintentional. In either event, without reco urse to complete inspection—certainly, by
new technological means, as far as is possibl e—the adoption of this bill in its present
form will mean that New Zealand has no means at all of intercepting or preventing such
threats.
That is a risk that I would suggest to me mbers is too great to be countenanced. The
SmartGate may not seem so smart after all if we  allow it to let in a virus that devastates
our pork industry or a moth that wipes out our pine forests. For these reasons New
Zealand First cannot support this bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: The Green Party is also unable to support this
bill, the Biosecurity Law Reform Bill. The Green Party is very, very concerned about
biosecurity, and we often, and for many y ears, have been pushing the issue of
inadequate biosecurity by successive Government s. We have seen pest after pest come
in, affecting different industries and affecting biodiversity in this country.
I was part of the early consultation on this bill, and it is clear that Biosecurity New
Zealand, as it was then, was really looking to  see whether it could have some better
systems and some better processes to look after biosecurity, and in some respects the
bill does address that. It is looking at how to do it in maybe a more user-pays way,
19 Jul 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 3787
which unfortunately leaves some glaring gaps , but not only that, it actually impacts on
industry in a very—how woul d you say it—hodgepodge way. It is a mix and match, all
over the place way of doing it. It is going to be inadequately resourced under the
Government-industry agreement system when  it is implemented, and that is being
attempted to be implemented now, under duress, in most of the industries.
Most of the changes may seem to be able  to enhance biosecurity outcomes in New
Zealand, but that would be only if biosecur ity was significantly better resourced, and
there is no intention of that. The Government  has not done it, and it did not do it in the
last Budget either.
The distributed responsibility for biosecurity management is, we say, a brave new
adventure for the Ministry of Primary Industries,  but it is one that wi ll blur the lines of
responsibility for biosecurity breaches. It is a more cooperative approach, and you
might say that will lead to some better bios ecurity outcomes, but it is actually blurring
the lines of responsibil ity, and we see that as  a very big risk. We see that as actually
quite sad.
I want to look at the real problems with biosecurity in New Zealand. The Minister for
Primary Industries has said it in this Hous e in recent months a couple of times: do we
want the same approach taken by our inte rnational markets, th e importers of our
produce into other markets? That was in response to the pig endogenous retrovirus more
recently, the pig issue—the thing that is in front of the court because it is so contentious.
The Minister expects that we will accept greater  risk into this country because of some
of our purported better exports. He says that we  need to prioritise, th at we will take up
the recommendations from the Pseudomonas syringae pv. Actinidiae investigation, and
that that will prioritise where biosecuri ty goes, depending on the importance of a
particular sector. That is a very narrow way of looking at it. It is a very risky way of
looking at it, because it puts it  down into just a few sectors that are seen as the sectors
where our economy is based. But that is our economy at the moment, on a really slack
commodity level. We have got pines, we have  got dairy, and if that  is all we are going
to rely on and we look the other way and no t at the depth that we need to around
biosecurity risk, we are not looking to the future for New Zealand.
I note that John Lancashire, the immediat e past president of  the New Zealand
Institute of Agricultural and Horticultural Science, in its recent publication lambasted
the Government—and previous Governments as  well, I must say—for the neo-liberal
approach that it has been taking to trade and biosecurity.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: What’s that mean?

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: That means that in recent years both major parties have
said they will do a little bit less regulation and they will do freer and freer trade, and that
means we are taking more risks about growing biosecurity threats. The slight loosening
of border controls has led to some very expensive search—

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: I am very happy to take a call on the
Biosecurity Law Reform Bill, a substantial pi ece of legislation that seeks to amend the
Biosecurity Act of 1993. Essentiall y, one of the things that th is bill seeks to do is to
bring the legislation up to date with th e technology that is av ailable in terms of
biosecurity in New Zealand.
As my colleagues have talked about at length, Labour does support this bill, although
we do have a couple of concer ns, which we have outlined, one of which my colleague
Damien O’Connor talked about earlier today. It was the Government-industry
agreements, and this is a concern for us. The other concern for us is that you can have
the best legislation in the wo rld, but if you do not properly re source it, it is not going to
work.
3788 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 19 Jul 2012
One of the things that my colleagues have talked about while we have been debating
this bill is the lack of resourcing that we  are seeing in this area of biosecurity. We are
seeing that Wellington Airpor t has not had a sniffer dog wo rking there since October
last year. We are seeing that there are cu ts, and this is of concern to everybody. We
support the efforts to increase our biosecu rity, because like most people, or like
everybody, really, in this House, and most Ne w Zealanders, we know that historically
New Zealand’s biosecurity and our protectin g of our land-based primary production—
our agricultural, our forestry, and our horticu ltural industries—is ab solutely crucial to
our economic survival, and, indeed, our econo mic development. Not only has it been
incredibly important to us hist orically as a nation but we se e, in Labour, that it is still
important to us today. It is very much part of our present.
This bill does recognise the vital im portance of biosecurity to our marine
environment, to our indigenous flora and fauna, and to human health. I think it is
interesting that we started de bating this bill last night, im mediately after the reading of
the exclusive economic zone legislation wher e we were seeing the House talking about
how it is that we could cont rol our exclusive economic zone . What we have here is a
piece of legislation that seeks to extend into that exclusive economic zone. So the
purpose of this bill, as I said, is to bring bi osecurity up to date to take into account the
technologies that are availabl e and had been there since th e passage of the legislation
that was passed in the 1990s.
The present bill that we have before us now  really goes back to when Labour was in
Government and the scare that the varroa m ite posed to an entir e industry. And, sadly,
since we have seen the scar e that the varroa mite posed to the honey industry, we have
seen several other scares, which members ha ve talked about during this debate. We
have seen the Pseudomonas syringae  pv. Actinidiae (Psa) incursion into the kiwifruit
industry—a $75 million problem. We have seen  the Queensland fruit fly in Auckland.
All those actions posed significant threats to New Zealand’s economic well-being.
The fruit fly alone could dest roy a $3 billion a year hort icultural industry. So these
might be very small organisms or very sm all insects, but they  are not very small
problems. These are things that we need to  protect against. This is why Labour more
than doubled the spending on biosecurity  between 1999 and 2008. We raised that
spending from $94 million to $187 million.
Then in 2003 Labour initiated the New Zealand Biotechnology Strategy, and this was
a very good piece of work. This strategy emphasise d the critical role, and this is what is
really important for me. This is a strate gy that emphasised the critical relationship
between science and biosecurity, and that sc ience needed to underpin what we were
doing in the area of protec ting our borders and in term s of our whole biosecurity
system.
This strategy identified four expectations of science in the field of biosecurity. It
emphasised that the science should be clos ely involved in the development of any
strategy, that the purchase of science shoul d be integrated acros s providers who are
working in this field, that the investment in science should be long term to ensure
maintenance of key capabilities, and that the priority for research to improve biosecurity
is understood. As someone who has worked in the research industry before entering this
House, I have seen very much that biosecur ity was at the forefront  of thinking in terms
of our horticultural and our primary production industries.
New technologies—many of which have been developed under this increased
funding that I have sketched out—are now be ing used in defending our borders, and the
legislation that we have before us now actua lly will enable us to make greater use of
these new technologies. It will ensure that a secure biosecu rity system from pre-border
management to pest management must be underpinned by this science that I was talking
19 Jul 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 3789
about, to support the so cial, the cultural, the environm ental, and the economic values
that are important to all of us  as New Zealanders, and that we must ensure that science
continues to underpin our approach to this system.
Our science in this area has a very st rong international reputation in fruit fly
protection, in eradication techniques, the use of baggage-securing X-ray technologies, in
fumigation technologies, in pesticide t echnologies, and in molecular diagnostic
techniques. These are all things that New Zealand scientists excel at and that we do very
good work at. We need to be able to use these technologies in the defence of our
borders. We have examples of these technolog ies being used to protect our borders, but
we also have examples of th ese technologies being commerci alised, and that is a spin-
off economic benefit to the New Zealand economy.
We have SniffertechTM, which was deve loped by the Crown re search institute
AgResearch, and it went on to be a very useful technology. Bios ecurity is a really
salient example of the importance of inves ting in science to our economy right across
the broad spectrum of how it is that we l ook at our economy. Our economic future is
dependent on this, and we must continue to innovate in this area. As I said, the purpose
of this bill is to enable us to use these innovations, these new technologies, and these
new bits of science.
The Biosecurity Act as it stands now does not reflect these sign ificant advances in
technologies that have taken place over the pa st decade, and that we anticipate we will
continue to make greater advances in. The pr esent legislation requires that some of the
acts be carried out in a manual way, when  time has moved on and we actually have
technology that could do a better job at this and actually do more to protect our borders.
For other functions there is uncertainty about whether the available or future
electronic technologies and systems can be used to support the prevention of biosecurity
risk. We must tidy that up, and one of the re asons that Labour is supporting this bill is
that it does precisely that. We need that legal certainty over the use of technology and
over the use of electronic de vices in defending our borders . The Ministry for Primary
Industries needs to have that certainty to improve, target, and manage the risks at our
borders. Visual inspection, as required in many ways now, will not pick up the
organisms that pose the threat, whether they ar e bacterial or viral su ch as Psa. We must
have a way to detect these. We have the te chnologies and we must be able to use them.
That is why Labour is supporting this bill at this reading. Thank you.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: I am pleased to make a
contribution to this Committee stage of the Biosecurity Law Reform Bill. Before I go
into talking around Part 1, I will say that bios ecurity is critical to our prosperity as a
nation. This bill is all about protecting our p ā, protecting our industries and our
livelihoods, protecting our brand, protecting ou r resources, and protecting our mana. So
Labour does support this bill. We have suppor ted it right since its introduction, but we
do have some reservations over a couple of aspects to the bill, particularly around the
Government-industry agreements, which my colleague Mr O’Connor has touched on.
I want to just take this opportunity to talk on Supplementary Order Paper 88, which
Te Ururoa Flavell has tabled. The proposed amendment is to insert new clause 8A,
which inserts new section 5A, “Principles of Treaty of Waitangi”, into the Biosecurity
Act. Labour supports this Supplementary Or der Paper and the incl usion of this new
clause. As we all know, the genesis for the principles of the Tr eaty of Waitangi came
out of the Treaty of Waitangi Act, its arch itect Matiu Rata, and the Labour Government
of those days, and it has been central to the whole modern-day era of the past 30 years
of Treaty settlements. There is a long line of Treaty jurisprudence around the principles
of the Treaty, but in terms of its inclusion in this bill it is very important in recognition
of Māori iwi and M āori as the tangata whenua and as ka itiaki for our natural resources,
3790 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 19 Jul 2012
and the partnership between M āori and the Crown. So we do support the inclusion of
this clause.
It is unequivocal in terms of the wording that “This Act must be interpreted and
administered so as to give effect to the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi.” I know Mr
Flavell has tabled another Supplementary Orde r Paper, but I believe that it might come
under a different part. We will discuss that at  a later time. But in terms of Part 1 and
new clause 8A, we support this Supplementary Order Paper.
Returning back to the thrust of this b ill, we do support the measures—for instance,
the new tools for more effective and efficient border biosecurity, placing more duties on
importers to take more reasonable steps in terms of their importation and compliance
with health standards, the modern-day fr amework for the use of information on risk
profiling; and one that was endorsed by my colleague Ms Mackey, which she spoke to
last evening, and that is th e expansion of the Biosecurity Act and its application to the
exclusive economic zone. So those are commendable measures in the bill.
I said that it is all about protecting our p ā. Having worked with M āori economic
interests, I know that M āori are significant stakeholders  in our primary industries,
whether it is our agricultural industries, our farms, our orchards, our marine farms,
fisheries, or forestry. In fact, the bulk of M āori assets are in the primary sector, and,
therefore, our trade and our ongoing viability in  those industries are really critical in
terms of our biosecurity. We are, in terms of the M āori sector, very, very keen to see
boosted protection of our pā.
That leads me on to the Government-industr y agreements. This is an area, I know,
where Labour does have reservations. It is a classic example, I guess, in terms of the
inequity between big industries and very sm all industries and the resourcing that is
required, but also the fact that these agreemen ts are between two par ties. We are seeing
it with the New Zealand pork industry at the moment. It is taking litigation against the
Government over the non-recogn ition of the scientific evidence that the industry is
putting forward in opposition to the lowering of the import standards for the some 800
tonnes of pork that comes into our country ev ery week. That is a critical issue for the
pork industry, and in terms of these Government -industry agreements, I think that it is a
classic example whereby the industry itself  cannot even get the Government to pay
recognition to its own scientif ic work. This is a Kiwi, Ne w Zealand industry, our pork
industry. I think we need to give a lot mo re consideration to the Government-industry
agreement provisions to make sure that there is a greater equity, and not too much cost
borne. There is a disproportionate  cost when the industries ar e so small, when it is a
small, fledgling, emerging export industry. We  all know that we want to broaden the
base of our exports sector, of our tradable  sector, so I think it would be good to just
focus on the Government-industry agreement area,  and make sure that that is tightly
drafted and meets the interests of the i ndustry itself. That re ally concludes my
contribution at this time. Kia ora.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: As I was pointing out, with the neo-liberal
approach, which is saying more and more free trade and sell out biosecurity for free
trade, John Lancashire was absolutely correct in pointing out that that is actually the
critical thing, the philo sophical thing, that is allowing bi osecurity risks to be increased.
As I have said, the Minister ha s repeatedly said that we need  to be open, we need to be
accepting more and more stuff coming in and mo re and more risk if we want to be
trading freely. But just today the World Tr ade Organization (WTO) came out and has
pointed out that for just that  material that is coming in, there are actually gaps around it
in terms of how it is being managed. The WTO is saying that that needs to be looked at.
The different agencies internationally, the WTO and the other agencies, need to be
working better to make sure that biosecurity works and that it is not seen as that trade
19 Jul 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 3791
barrier. Instead of taking the ap proach that it is always a trade barrier, we actually need
to look at biosecurity almost first. We defi nitely do need to look at it first, but this

items.speaker: Government has been saying
items.text: “No, no. We want  to open up, let more in, and take more
risks.” So it is very interesting that that cam e out today, while we ha ve got this bill, the
Biosecurity Law Reform Bill, in front of us that is quite shaky in terms of looking after
biosecurity here.
The other thing that has just happened, of course—and a colleague mentioned this
before—is the four new dogs, which is ver y, very good because he and the Green Party
had been repeatedly saying that there are not enough decent inspections at our ports, so
it is good to see th at there has been a media advisory out to say that there are four new
dogs out, and the breeding programme is exp ecting to see 11 new Labradors graduate
from training this year, as pa rt of a move to bolster biosecu rity in this country. That is
absolutely fantastic. There is no doubt about it. There are some major gaps, and they are
being filled. But I would ask how many more staff are going to be coming back into
MAF Biosecurity New Zealand. How many more dollars and how many more resources
are going to go into making sure we can do an adequate job? Will the increased staffing,
assuming there is a handler for each of those dogs, because there needs to be, exceed the
successive losses from successive Government s in successive years of backtracking
around biosecurity investment in this country?
I will just point out some of the losses that  we can expect to get if we carry on down
this track of liberalising and loosening biosecurity by not res ourcing it properly.
Horticulture New Zealand a couple of years back did a look at what would happen if
fruit fly got into various regi ons, and pointed out that in  the Bay of Plenty the loss
would be $820 million and 3,430 jobs lost, Hawke’s Bay $390 million and just over
3,000 jobs lost, and in Nelson $265 million an d 1,945 jobs lost. Yes, the Government
did jump when a male fruit fly sprung up in  Auckland. We also know what the cost was
of that. That would not have happened if we had better port co ntrols. Pysllids are
another one, affecting the spud industry, tomatoes, capsicums, and tamarillos—the
Solanum family industry. It has cost the industry already something like $250 million in
lost production, markets, and production costs, yet there is no more money and there is
nothing happening, really, in terms of reduci ng those risks. Yes, there are some dogs—
that is a little bit of catch-up—but there is no more loot going in there to make this
better.
I come back to the aspect that I touched on earlier, in terms of the prioritisation of
biosecurity in New Zealand. Instead of a se rious blanket approach of dealing with
biosecurity fully from a Government appro ach, we have got a bundl e of industries that
will all suffer significantly. We have got the forestry industry, which is incredibly
vulnerable, particularly with its monoculture.

Ayes 98
New Zealand National 59; New Zealand Labour 34; M āori Party 3; ACT New
Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Noes 23
Green Party 14; New Zealand First 8; Mana 1.
Amendments agreed to.
Part 1 as amended agreed to.
Part 2  Amendments relating to ballast water
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman) : I have to
acknowledge my good colleague Rino Tirikate ne there. I slightly misled him on a
debate. I am sure he will have the chance to put his views to the Committee on this part.

items.speaker: Hon Craig Foss
items.text: Do you wear that tie on the West Coast, Damien?
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR : Absolutely. It takes more than clothes to maketh a
man down there.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: That’s why he never made it.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR : That is right. As I said, Labour is supporting the
Biosecurity Law Reform Bill, but we do have some major problems with it and with the
resourcing of biosecurity across this country. In speaking to the next part of the bill, and
particularly in regard to the formation of pest-management strategies—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: No.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR: Clause 76? Sorry, Mr Chairman, I am—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Ballast water and the marine environment.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR : Ah, yes. Going back to the marine environment
clauses—

items.speaker: Hon Craig Foss
items.text: Loosen the tie. Come on—loosen the tie.
19 Jul 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 3793
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR: That is what a pink tie does to you.
Can I say we actually welcom e having provisions in the Biosecurity Act, finally,
around ballast water. It is a situation that I am familiar with because going back some
20 years, in fact, there was an application in  South Westland to export fresh water. That
was out of Jacksons Bay. Anyone who has been down there knows th at it is a pristine
environment. I know that the Chairman, Mr Roy, has been down there many times. One
of the issues that arose then—and it has not  come up that often—was ballast water and
what the potential impact could be of balla st water being tipped into Jacksons Bay by
boats that had set out from Singapore or some Middle Eastern port, gone down there,
and put that water out there, bringing with it all the pests and diseas es. At that time no
one had really identified the risk. It was put up as an argument primarily by the green
movement at that time—way before the Green Party. But there were environmental
groups that were concerned, legitimately, about what might happen down there through
ballast water being put into that bay. I ha ve to say that was one of a number of
arguments and issues that actually put that whole project on hold. I am sure that at some
stage we probably will be exporting fresh water from this country as its value increases.
The issue, though, is ballast water, the management of it, and ensuring that we do not
bring pests into this country unnecessarily. I do not think we can ever guarantee that we
will not bring in something, or that we have not brought it in. Undaria, which is a
seaweed that has some commercial uses but has been deemed a weed, was mostly
brought in through the ballast water of boats. The question I have in this area—again,
because we have a Government that refuses to properly resource MAF Biosecurity New
Zealand—is whether, with all these regulati ons and these improvements that we accept
are needed, effectively we may not offer any more protection for the New Zealand
marine environment with the passage of this bill than there was before, and that would
be a problem. We have here in clause 76 new Part 19A, “Protection of marine
environment from ballast water”. Ballast wa ter means, as we know , anything picked up
to stabilise a boat on its way to New Zeala nd with a cargo. Cargoe s change in weight,
and, obviously, the ships need to take on board water to make sure they do not tip over.
What we have done here is put in place defences for people who think they took all
reasonable steps to minimise any potential risk  to New Zealand, as the other part of the
bill is quite prescriptive.
I have to say that we hope we have got it right, because as good as the chair of the
Primary Production Committee is, I am not sure —maybe he will take a call. I hope he
will get up and explain. I know he has been fairly diligent all the way through this
process, and he probably has read this bill a number of times, so he would be able to get
up and explain each and every single part of it.
Can I say that what we do have in there, as well, under Part 3—I am sorry, we going
up to clause 78 only. I apologise for that, Mr Chairman. I was just trying to rush the bill
through. I do not want to prolong it any longer than necessary. The clauses up to clause
78 deal with marine pollution, as well, which is  another serious issue.  It is one that has
been overlooked internationally, I would sugge st. I am not sure whether this provision
puts us at the forefront of ballast water ma nagement internationally, but if we have a
stricter regime for boats coming into our territo rial waters, then so be it. There are, we
are told, ways of flushing ballast  water as ships are in transit. As to whether that occurs
or not, I am guessing there is probably an o ffset in energy use and maybe the speed of
the boat in doing that, and we are concerned that, in fact, it might not occur. Hence the
heavy fines of up to $200,000, or imprisonment for up to 2 years. That is quite a penalty
for someone who discharges ba llast water in breach of th e regulations that we are
allowing to pass here. I think it , quite rightfully, says to each and every ship owner, to
the people in charge of those ships: “If you come into New Zealand, we want to keep
3794 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 19 Jul 2012
our marine environment free of any unwanted pests and organisms. So we will pass this
bill, we will allow regulations to be put in place, and we are going to hammer you if you
don’t do it.”
I think this part is a good part of th e bill—we acknowledge the Government for it—
and that is why we will support it. But, ag ain, if we do not have the resources to
properly police and implement these regulations , then they effectively mean nothing. In
this area it is not going to be easy. In spite of, I guess, the ship companies’
determination to reduce the number of ports th eir ships come into, there will be ships in
our territorial waters, over our fisheries ar eas, that may not abide by these regulations.
So we welcome this part of the bill.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere): I am so excited to talk about this bill,
the Biosecurity Law Reform Bill. I am going to confine my comments to new Part 19A
in clause 76. But before I do s o, I want to tell yo u why I am excited about Part 2 of this
particular bill with reference to ballast water. The other day my colleague the Hon
Damien O’Connor took us to a dairy farm and he had us stand in front of this big, huge,
open septic tank. There were tw o or three of them, and he said to us: “Now, boys, have
a sniff of that.” So we took deep breaths and then, before we knew it, the Hon Damien
O’Connor said to us: “That’s the smell of money.” I could not believe it at first, because
I just thought it was the smell of cow poop, but I now recognise th at the point he was
making was the value of our agricultural indus try. What I noticed was that they had the
cow waste go from one septic tank to the ne xt—there are three or four of them—and at
the bottom they then recycle the clean water.  What they would normally do is disperse
that throughout the farm.
In terms of this particular bill, in regard to ballast water, “Ballast water means water
with its suspended matter taken on board a ship to control the ship’s trim, list, draught,
stability, or stresses.” The bi g question is where that water comes from, because if it is
water that comes off the fina l open septic tank, then ther e is going to be concern,
particularly if it is  coming from another country, and we may have to ask questions
about who owns the water, w ho has the rights to the water that goes on these particular
ships. We may even have to have a secret meeting to decide who has the rights to the
water that comes from that ship.
I am particularly pleased because in new section 246B it states: “(1) ballast water
may be discharged from a ship only in accordance with the applicable marine protection
rules.” I believe that the farmers, our aquacu lture sector, our forest sector, and our wine
industry are going to be quite excited about this particular bill—all 264 pages of it—
because they are going to have to hire employees, consultants, and other people to try to
make sense of what is in this bill.
Do not get me wrong. At the end of the da y, as the Hon Damien O’Connor says, we
support the bill. But in terms of having the m easures that will enable us to, hopefully,
protect and continue to safeguard our borders for the sake of our valuable industry, we
really cannot have the Govern ment shirk its responsibilitie s. So I suppose, with the
farmers who would be listening in to this debate, the respons ibility still falls on them to
hold this Government to account. At the e nd of the day, when Mr Damien O’Connor
says, with reference to our agricultural s ector, that that is the smell of money, it
underlines the fact that we ha ve got a very valuable industry that we have to be
protective of. [ Interruption] At the end of the day, I agree that the penalties that have
been imposed of $200,000—“a fine not exceeding $200,000; and … if the offence is a
continuing one, a further fine not exceeding $10,000 …”—send a clear signal. It
imposes responsibility on the importers, but it still should no t allow this Government to
shirk its responsibility, because ultimately the Government is our representative and has
the duty to protect and safeguard our borders . If that does not happen—and we have
19 Jul 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 3795
already seen examples of what has occurred. I will give you just some examples in
terms of what has happened. The la test independent report on the Pseudomonas
syringae pv. Actinidiae disease shows it will cost our border—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! I am having difficulty following the
member’s logic, but this is quite specific. So I ask the member to contain himself to
clauses 76 to 78.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO : The point that I am making in terms of the ballast water
clauses is that there are serious concerns about ensuring that the ballast water is not
released in our shores. I will give you anot her example. In 1990 a ship by the name of
the Naomi travelled between the islands of Samoa and American Samoa. Because they
did not ensure that there were safeguards and protection on what was carried on that
cargo ship—

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: We have now moved on to Part 2
of the Biosecurity Law Reform Bill and we  are dealing with the marine environment
and biosecurity. As my colleagues have mentioned, we support this part and the
provisions that are contained in  it—in particular, the fact th at there are stern penalties
imposed for breaches of conditions in terms of discharge of ballast water.
Having worked at one stage in the fishi ng industry, I know that  there is a lot of
activity that goes on with thos e vessels, and the vessels ar e not contained purely in the
New Zealand 12-mile or exclusive economic zo ne. We do have a lot of ships that go up
to the Pacific, out of zone, and that does not even mention the amount of merchant trade
ships that go into our ports each and ever y day—the lifeblood of our main port towns—
and the emerging and burgeoning tourism cruise  ship industry. It is very positive,
actually, that we do see so many more cruise  ships coming in during the peak summer
periods.
It is commendable now that we have some  biosecurity provisi ons in relation to
ballast water, and I would just like to say th at perhaps Te Ururoa Flavell could have put
in some conditions around consultation with tangata whenua, given that we have large
investments in the marine industr y, and there is a lot of the M āori asset base that is
dependent on the marine environment. Perhaps he could have extended those
consultation provisions he ha d in his Supplementary Or der Paper, which we did
support, but, obviously, it was not agreed to. But we do suppor t that idea that there be
greater consultation with tangata whenua, pa rticularly around things like the national
pest management strategy, regional strategies, and the like.
Progress reported.
Report adopted.

Viet Nam—Delegation, National Assembly 
Mr SPEAKER: Honourable members, I have much pleasure in informing the House 
that a parliamentary delegation from the Na tional Assembly of Viet Nam, led by Mr 
Nguyen Van Hien, Chairman of the Committee on Judiciary, is present in the gallery. I 
am sure members would wish that the delegation be welcomed. 
BUSINESS STATEMENT 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House) : When the House resumes on 
Tuesday, 24 July the Government will comp lete the Dairy Industry Restructuring 
Amendment Bill and a number of first readings on the Order Paper, including the 
Families Commission Amendment Bill and the Companies and Limited Partnerships 
Amendment Bill. Wednesday is a members’ day. The Business Committee has also 
determined that the House will take extended hours on Wednesday, 25 July, effective 
from 9 a.m. on Thursday, 26 July, for the third readings of the Maraeroa A and B 
Blocks Claims Settlement Bill and the Maraeroa A and B Blocks Incorporation Bill, the 
Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill, the Ng āti Mākino Claims Settlement Bill, and 
the Rongowhataata Claims Settlement Bill. 
Hon TREVOR MALLARD (Labour—Hutt South) : Can I ask the Leader of the 
House two questions: first of a ll, to confirm that those third readings will run into the 
afternoon of Thursday next week, as well as the extended Wednesday; and, also, to give 
an assurance, as far as the following week is concerned, that if we do go on to the liquor 
legislation, there will be plenty of notice because of the conscience vote nature of it? 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House) : Two things. I thank the 
shadow Leader of the House for those questi ons. It is a good opportun ity to clarify that 
under the Standing Orders the Government, by agreement with the Business Committee, 
in this case will call for extended hours on Wednesday, 25 July, because what we are 
doing is extending the Wednesday into the Thur sday. In effect, we will deal with those 
bills on Thursday morning, running through into the afternoon. Ther e will still be a 
question time. I will shortly seek leave for the House to sit beyond the 6 o’clock mark, 
should we require it, to complete those third readings. 
On the issue of the alcohol bill, there are a number of points in the bill that will be of 
interest to members across the House. I thin k it is desirable that we have a broad 
discussion at the Business Committee. My proposal  is that we will have that discussion 
next Tuesday—and I will try to get some information to members of the committee 
prior to that time—when we might get some agreement on how we could satisfy 
everybody’s requirements around that debate. 
SITTINGS OF THE HOUSE 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (L eader of the House) : So that we get everything 
done in sequence, I will now seek leave th at should the debate on the bills that the 
Business Committee has agreed will be dea lt with under extended hours next week 
progress beyond 6 o’clock on the Thursday, th e House will continue beyond 6 o’clock 
for the conclusion of the third readings. 
3746 Sittings of the House 19 Jul 2012 
Hon TREVOR MALLARD (Labour—Hutt South) : I raise a point of order, Mr 
Speaker. I think we also indicated that we might deal with some flexibility around the 1 
o’clock time, if we were coming to the end of the debate on one of those bills. 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House) : That is true. We essentially 
are splitting the debate on these five bill s into morning and afternoon sessions. I think 
the leave should be that if either of those sessions requires the House to sit for a short 
time beyond the normal rising time, we should do so until the conclusion of the debate 
on the bill in progress. 
Mr SPEAKER : Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objection? 
There is no objection.  
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Water Rights—Prime Minister’s Statements 
1. GRANT ROBERTSON (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Prime Minister : 
Does he stand by all his statements regarding water ownership, rights and interests? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister)  on behalf of the Prime Minister: 
Yes. 
Grant Robertson: Can he confirm the joint announcem ent he made last night with 
the M āori Party leadership that no matter what the outcome of the tribunal and 
subsequent court action, he will not legislate, even if that outcome was that M āori had a 
proprietary-type right over water? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The Prime Minister stands by the statements made in the 
statement that was released. 
Grant Robertson: Can he confirm that his agreem ent to not legislate against M āori 
rights and interests in water has, in fact , already been broken by the Mixed Ownership 
Model Bill, which has passed through Parliame nt and allows for th e partial sale of 
entities like Mighty River Power th at have rights and interests in water that affect all 
New Zealanders, including Māori? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : No, the Mixed Ownership Model Bill does not do that. In 
fact, it includes the preservation of section 9 of the State-Owned Enterprises Act and its 
references to the Treaty of Waitangi. What th e Prime Minister is doing is quite different 
from what the previous Labour Government di d, and that is we are building confidence 
around discussion with Māori about their rights and interests, rather than overreacting— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! That was beyond the question asked. 
Grant Robertson : Can he confirm that it is hi s Government’s intention that no 
matter what the outcome of the Waitangi  Tribunal and subsequent court action—
whatever rights it may decide M āori have in terms of water—his Government will not 
legislate in that regard? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The Prime Minister stands by the statement in the statement 
that was released last night. It is the Gove rnment’s expectation that—well, put it this 
way: the member is probably not correctly  connecting any outcome from the Waitangi 
Tribunal with any outcome from the court action, because the court action is much more 
likely to be focused on preventing the sale of assets going ahead, rather than any 
particular aspect of Māori rights and interests. 
Grant Robertson: Does he agree with Tariana Turia that it was a misconception that 
this claim is about the owne rship of water; if so, why did he continue to make 
statements about his opposition to the ownershi p of water, if not to  just raise tension 
around the issue? 
19 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 3747 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The issue of ownership was actually raised by the claimants. 
In fact, we have seen claimants, I thi nk, discussing it publicly  recently. The Prime 
Minister stands by his restatement of the longstanding view of New Zealand’s 
Governments and jurisprudence that no one owns the water. 
Hon Trevor Mallard: In light of the indemnity granted for Treaty matters to private 
shareholders of the to-be-privatised State-owned enterprises under the mixed ownership 
model legislation passed recently, does that mean that all risk from court action now lies 
with the Crown; if so, why did his Minister of Finance not record that unspecified fiscal 
risk as part of the Budget documentation currently being considered by the House? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: It has always been the case that the risks or costs associated 
with Treaty settlements are matters between the Crown and iwi. But,  again, I think this 
member, like the other, is getting ahead of himself over whether or not the courts are 
likely to be settling the issue of M āori rights and interests. There is a prospect of court 
action. That court action is much more likely to be related to injuncting the sale process. 
It is unlikely that the courts them selves would set out to determine M āori rights and 
interests. If they did, that could take quite a long time. 
Grant Robertson: Is it correct that the reasons he raised the spectre of ownership of 
water by M āori were to divert pub lic attention from his hugely unpopular asset sales 
programme and to inflame divisions about Treaty issues, and when will he apologise for 
this divisive behaviour? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : I think the member is overstating his case there. The fact is 
claimants have gone to the tribunal, they ha ve made a range of claims, and some of 
them have expressed those claims as owners hip of the water. The Prime Minister just 
clearly restated, in the light of that action in the tribunal, what the longstanding position 
of New Zealand Governments has been, and it will remain so. Obviously, there is pretty 
broad public interest in whether the Waitangi Tribunal is or is not going to be contesting 
the ownership of water. 
State-owned Energy Companies and Air New Zealand, Sales—Cost as at July 2012 
2. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green) to the Minister of Finance: What 
has been the total cost to date of exte nding and implementing the Government’s asset 
sales programme, which it calls the Mixed Ownership Model? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : As I said in answer to a similar 
question last month, the total amounts of th e contracts are commercially sensitive 
because the Government intends to renegotia te those contracts fo r each partial share

SOCIAL SECURITY (YOUTH SUPPORT AND WORK FOCUS) AMENDMENT 
BILL 
Third Reading 
Hon PAULA BENNETT (Minister for Social Development) : I move, That the 
Social Security (Youth Support and Work Focus) Amendmen t Bill be now read a third 
time. Doing nothing about benefit dependency is no longer an option. For too long the 
system has let thousands of New Zealande rs languish on benefits, with no hope, no 
support, and no encouragement to live and lead a better life. In fact , the welfare system 
itself has failed too many New Zealanders. This Government will not stand by and let 
that continue. The bill be fore the House today con tinues the significant and 
comprehensive reforms this Government has introduced to modernise the welfare 
system. It started with Future Focus in 2010 an d we are following it up with this bill, 
before introducing a third tranche of welfare reform later this year that will contain the 
most significant changes.  
The changes we are making will reset ob ligations and expect ations, introducing a 
level of fairness that is long overdue. The statistics have been  telling us for years that 
welfare dependence is intergenerational. This causes a loss of hope and a lack of 
ambition for adults and for their children  in so many ways. One hundred and seventy 
thousand New Zealanders have spent most of  the last decade on welfare. You cannot 
tell me that that is good for them as i ndividuals, good for their families, or, certainly, 
any good for their children. We simply cannot continue to spend up to $8 billion a year 
to support 12 percent of the working-age population. I cannot ask taxpayers to support a 
system that continually grows, but does not address the causes of dependence, at the 
expense of health, education, and other priorities that taxpayers might like us to make.  
I am not convinced that the left sees a pr oblem with this level of dependence, but I 
am convinced there is a difference in philo sophy when it comes to welfare. The left 
creates dependence; the right creates indepe ndence. We would rather give them the 
tools and the support to be independent. The right will incentivise, while the left are 
busy with sympathising. This is not about a lack of compassion. I have a huge amount 
of respect for people who are raising their families with little money. I just want them to 
have more. We could do nothi ng, as the left would prefer , and that means leaving the 
19 Jul 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 3761 
320,000 New Zealanders on welfare, with no hope  of a better life. I simply refuse to do 
that.  
When listening to the debate on these reforms it is clear that some have no faith 
whatsoever in the ability of New Zealanders to get off welfare and provide for 
themselves. On this side of the House, qui te frankly, we see that as demeaning. We 
believe in people and their ability to succeed and better their situation, and we believe in 
providing them with the support so that they  can do so. We do not believe in leaving 
people on the scrap heap. To continue simp ly paying a 17-year-old sole mother a 
weekly sum of money and give her no other support would quite frankly, in my view, 
be irresponsible. We will not do that. To wr ite off single women as unable to support 
themselves financially, simply because they are women, would be ignorant. We will not 
do that. To allow people to just give up and opt out of work would be a failure of any 
Government, and we will not do that. National will modernise the welfare system with a 
clear work focus that applies to a far greater number of people.  
We will take a completely new approach with young people. They will be required to 
be in education or training to get a benefit. Their bills will be paid directly. Money for 
food will be loaded on to payment cards, inst ead of giving them cash. They will have to 
complete budgeting and/or parenting program mes, if appropriate . They will receive 
small cash incentives for meeting these milestones. Instead of having a solely financial 
relationship with Work and Income, teen pa rents, along with other young people, will 
have a youth service provider or private work er working alongside them. That provider 
will help them navigate issues like accommodation, bills, getting access to education or 
training, and upskilling. Teen parents will ge t vital childcare. We are putting aside $80 
million for this, so there is no barrier to th em getting the education or training they 
need.  
This bill will require sole parents with  children over 14 to look for full-time work, 
and will require sole parents with children over 5 to look for part-time work. This bill 
will require those parents to start preparing themselves, in advance, for this change. 
This bill removes the sexist  and discriminatory policy th at has seen the women alone 
and widows benefits existing well beyond a time when they were necessary. These 
benefits effectively said that a woman c ould not fend for herself without a man, and I 
think that is just archaic. We are modernising welfare. We  are providing more support, 
and we will be expecting something back. We have changed the commencement date of 
30 July 2012 for the youth package changes to 20 August 2012. Changes to the widows 
benefit, women alone benefit, and DPB come into effect in October of this year.  
As I have mentioned, the bill introduces a new system of support, obligations, and 
financial assistance for young peopl e and teen parents. The aim of this is to balance 
support and obligations in a way that will improve social  outcomes for young people. 
This is new; it is a different approach to a longstanding problem. Never before has 
anyone looked at the benefit pipeline and put such a huge i nvestment into those very 
young people who are likely to go on to benefit. Currently, there are around 3,000 16 
and 17-year-olds and 16 to 18-year-old  parents on a benefit, and around 14,000 young 
people aged 16 to 17 years wh o are considered to be “neets”—not in education, 
employment, or training. We are determined to stop the track on to benefit. The changes 
in this bill will reduce the risk of long-te rm benefit dependency for teenagers, and 
ensure they have better outcomes and opportuni ties. The best way to do this is through 
work and training, and we are investing $148 m illion over 4 years for youth services to 
achieve this, including that very necessary wraparound support.  
The left has criticised this investment a lot. I stand by it. We are going to have youth-
focused providers who are the experts in working with young people, motivating them, 
and helping them to turn th eir lives round. We are being fl exible and innovative in how

JACINDA ARDERN (Labour): I am pleased to rise on behalf of the Labour Party 
and give what I think is a very considered  response from our party to this piece of

between science and biosecurity, and that sc ience needed to underpin what we were 
doing in the area of protec ting our borders and in term s of our whole biosecurity 
system.  
This strategy identified four expectations of science in the field of biosecurity. It 
emphasised that the science should be clos ely involved in the development of any 
strategy, that the purchase of science shoul d be integrated acros s providers who are 
working in this field, that the investment in science should be long term to ensure 
maintenance of key capabilities, and that the priority for research to improve biosecurity 
is understood. As someone who has worked in the research industry before entering this 
House, I have seen very much that biosecur ity was at the forefront  of thinking in terms 
of our horticultural and our primary production industries.  
New technologies—many of which have been developed under this increased 
funding that I have sketched out—are now be ing used in defending our borders, and the 
legislation that we have before us now actua lly will enable us to make greater use of 
these new technologies. It will ensure that a secure biosecu rity system from pre-border 
management to pest management must be underpinned by this science that I was talking 
19 Jul 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 3789 
about, to support the so cial, the cultural, the environm ental, and the economic values 
that are important to all of us  as New Zealanders, and that we must ensure that science 
continues to underpin our approach to this system.  
Our science in this area has a very st rong international reputation in fruit fly 
protection, in eradication techniques, the use of baggage-securing X-ray technologies, in 
fumigation technologies, in pesticide t echnologies, and in molecular diagnostic 
techniques. These are all things that New Zealand scientists excel at and that we do very 
good work at. We need to be able to use these technologies in the defence of our 
borders. We have examples of these technolog ies being used to protect our borders, but 
we also have examples of th ese technologies being commerci alised, and that is a spin-
off economic benefit to the New Zealand economy.  
We have SniffertechTM, which was deve loped by the Crown re search institute 
AgResearch, and it went on to be a very useful technology. Bios ecurity is a really 
salient example of the importance of inves ting in science to our economy right across 
the broad spectrum of how it is that we l ook at our economy. Our economic future is 
dependent on this, and we must continue to innovate in this area. As I said, the purpose 
of this bill is to enable us to use these innovations, these new technologies, and these 
new bits of science.  
The Biosecurity Act as it stands now does not reflect these sign ificant advances in 
technologies that have taken place over the pa st decade, and that we anticipate we will 
continue to make greater advances in. The pr esent legislation requires that some of the 
acts be carried out in a manual way, when  time has moved on and we actually have 
technology that could do a better job at this and actually do more to protect our borders.  
For other functions there is uncertainty about whether the available or future 
electronic technologies and systems can be used to support the prevention of biosecurity 
risk. We must tidy that up, and one of the re asons that Labour is supporting this bill is 
that it does precisely that. We need that legal certainty over the use of technology and 
over the use of electronic de vices in defending our borders . The Ministry for Primary 
Industries needs to have that certainty to improve, target, and manage the risks at our 
borders. Visual inspection, as required in many ways now, will not pick up the 
organisms that pose the threat, whether they ar e bacterial or viral su ch as Psa. We must 
have a way to detect these. We have the te chnologies and we must be able to use them. 
That is why Labour is supporting this bill at this reading. Thank you.
